To ensure each report can be published on the College website for applicants to compare
questions.explanation: Section 2.3 states that Course Coordinators use a set template so reports allow cross-comparison of data, enabling an overall College collective annual report to be constructed.
questions.source_excerpt: Through a set template, Course Coordinators construct reports in a way that allows for cross-comparison of data, thus enabling an overall College collective annual report to be constructed;

questions.question: According to the Annual Monitoring Policy, what should individual programme reports identify and include?
options: Staff sickness absence totals and the planned recruitment of new lecturers
The programme's marketing spend and its targets for next year's student applications
Key actions to be taken in the following year, and student satisfaction indicators
A list of students with outstanding tuition fees and their agreed payment plans
questions.explanation: Section 2.5 states that individual programme reports should identify key actions to be taken during the following year and should include student satisfaction indicators.
questions.source_excerpt: Individual programme reports should identify key actions to be taken during the following year and should include student satisfaction indicators;

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which body considers programme and College reports and makes recommendations as to future development?
options: The Assessment Board
The Academic Board
The Board of Directors
The Staff Consultative Forum
questions.explanation: Section 2.6 states that programme and College reports will be considered by the Academic Board, which will make recommendations as to future development.
questions.source_excerpt: Programme and College reports will be considered by the Academic Board which will make recommendations as to future development;

questions.question: According to the Annual Monitoring Policy, who is responsible for overseeing the smooth running of Programmes and has regular contact with the Course Coordinators?
options: The Director of Quality Assurance and Compliance
The Chair of the Programme Committee
The Senior Tutor for Academic Standards
The Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring
questions.explanation: Section 3.1.3 states that the Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring (HoPAM) is responsible for overseeing the smooth running of Programmes and has regular contact with the Course Coordinators.
questions.source_excerpt: The Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring (HoPAM) is responsible for overseeing the smooth running of Programmes and has regular contact with ... the Course Coordinators.

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, who is required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report, and how often?
options: Unit Tutors, after each instance of unit delivery ends
Course Coordinators, annually each January
Programme Leaders, once per term, using the template
The HoPAM, before each monthly PEG meeting
questions.explanation: Section 3.1.2 states that Programme Leaders are required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template.
questions.source_excerpt: Programme Leaders are required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template,

questions.question: According to the Annual Monitoring Policy, what does the practice of monthly oral reports and termly written reports to the PEG facilitate?
options: Annual approval of each programme's budget and staffing levels by the College Oversight Board
A timely response to issues arising from programmes, and the dissemination of good practice
Formal confirmation of unit grades before the Assessment Board releases them to students
Replacement of the Programme Annual Monitoring Report for smaller programmes
questions.explanation: Section 3.1.1 states that monthly oral and termly written reports to the PEG facilitate a timely response to issues arising from programmes and the dissemination of good practice.
questions.source_excerpt: oral reports are made to the PEG on a monthly basis and written reports are submitted each term. This facilitates a timely response to issues arising from programmes, as well as the dissemination of good practice;

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy's reporting arrangement for Unit Evaluation Reports (UERs), what is the review cycle?
options: Annually, by November
Termly, by the final week
Annually, by September
Annually, by the end of July
questions.explanation: The UER reporting arrangement in section 3.2.3 sets the review cycle as annually, by November.
questions.source_excerpt: Reporting Arrangement: ... Review Cycle: Annually, by November ... Author: ... Unit Tutor ... Output: ... Unit Evaluation Report

questions.question: According to the Annual Monitoring Policy's reporting arrangement, for whom is the Unit Evaluation Report (UER) intended?
options: The awarding body and the Office for Students
Students who studied the unit
The Programme Committee and QESC
Human Resources and the tutor's line manager
questions.explanation: The UER reporting arrangement in section 3.2.3 states that it is intended for the Programme Committee and QESC.
questions.source_excerpt: Output: ... Unit Evaluation Report ... Intended for: Programme Committee and QESC

questions.question: According to the Annual Monitoring Policy, what period does a Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) reflect on?
options: The preceding academic year, produced at the end of each academic year
The current term only, produced in the final week of each term
The last three academic years, produced at each periodic review
A single unit's delivery, produced after each Assessment Board meets
questions.explanation: Section 3.3.1 states that a PAMR is a reflective report of the preceding academic year, produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme.
questions.source_excerpt: A Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) is a reflective report of the preceding academic year, produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme offered by the College.

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, besides going to the Academic Board and the College Oversight Board, where is the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR) also shared?
options: At student induction sessions and applicant open days
In the student handbook and on the public website
At Programme Committee Meetings and All Staff Meetings
At Assessment Board and External Examiner meetings
questions.explanation: Section 3.4.2 states that the CAMR is also shared at Programme Committee Meetings and All Staff Meetings.
questions.source_excerpt: It is also shared at Programme Committee Meetings and All Staff Meetings.

questions.question: According to the Annual Monitoring Policy, which group attends both the Academic Board and the Programme Committee, in the interest of a transparent monitoring process?
options: Employer representatives
Student Representatives
Alumni association members
Awarding body observers
questions.explanation: Section 3.4.2 states that, in the interest of a transparent monitoring process, both the Academic Board and the Programme Committee are attended by Student Representatives.
questions.source_excerpt: In the interest of operating a transparent monitoring process, both the Academic Board and the Programme Committee are attended by Student Representatives.

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, who authors the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR) and its action plan?
options: The Course Coordinators for each programme
The Chair of the College Oversight Board
The Clerk to the Academic Board
The Principal or his/her designated person
questions.explanation: The CAMR reporting arrangement in section 3.4.3 names the Principal or his/her designated person as author of the Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan.
questions.source_excerpt: Author: ... Principal or his/her designated person ... Output: ... Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan

questions.question: A London Churchill College programme is run with an awarding body and is also accredited by a professional body. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, whose requirements does the College acknowledge in maintaining that programme's academic standards?
options: The awarding body's regulations only, as professional bodies are out of scope
The awarding body's regulations, the OfS, and the professional body's expectations
The professional body's expectations only, as these override awarding body rules
The Academic Board's own regulations only, as it approves all programme standards
questions.explanation: Section 1.1 states that, in maintaining academic standards, the College acknowledges the regulations of its awarding bodies, the OfS and the expectations of external professional, statutory and other regulatory bodies.
questions.source_excerpt: In maintaining these standards, the College acknowledges the regulations of its awarding bodies, the OfS and the expectations of external professional, statutory and other regulatory bodies;

questions.question: Students on your programme have raised concerns about the library and learning resources available to them. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, how should resources be treated in the programme's monitoring?
options: They are left out, as resources are reviewed separately by library staff outside monitoring
They are left out unless the concerns are submitted as a formal student complaint
They are reported only to the College Oversight Board, as resources are a budget matter
They are included, as monitoring covers the resources available to staff and students
questions.explanation: Section 2.1 states that all programmes must be monitored and that monitoring includes the learning, library and other resources available to staff and students.
questions.source_excerpt: All programmes must be monitored and include student, staff and external feedback, an analysis of grades and other academic performance indicators, learning, library, and other resources available to staff and students;

questions.question: Following the Academic Board's recommendations, the Principal's Executive Group (PEG) is tracking agreed changes to a programme. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, when does the PEG report back to the Academic Board on these changes?
options: Once a term, alongside each Termly Monitoring Report
Once a year in March, together with the annual CAMR
At such times as the Academic Board may require
Monthly, as part of the HoPAM's oral report to the Board
questions.explanation: Section 2.7 states that the PEG tracks and monitors suggested and agreed changes throughout the following year and reports back to the Academic Board at such times as the Board may require.
questions.source_excerpt: The Principal's Executive Group (PEG) will track and monitor suggested and agreed changes throughout the following year and report back to the Academic Board at such times as the Board may require.

questions.question: The Principal's Executive Group (PEG) is meeting this month. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, how does the Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring (HoPAM) provide oversight of programmes at that meeting?
options: By tabling each Programme Leader's Termly Monitoring Report for the PEG's formal approval
By giving an oral report at the PEG meeting, which typically takes place once per month
By presenting a written digest of the Unit Evaluation Reports completed that month
By submitting the Course Coordinators' draft PAMRs for the PEG to sign off
questions.explanation: Section 3.1.3 states that the HoPAM provides oversight of programmes through an oral report at each PEG meeting, which typically takes place once per month.
questions.source_excerpt: The HoPAM provides oversight of programmes through an oral report at each PEG meeting, which typically takes place once per month.

questions.question: A Unit Tutor wants to complete the Unit Evaluation Report (UER) before the unit's results have been to LCC's Assessment Board. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, why does the UER rely on the Assessment Board?
options: The form comments on the unit statistics, which are provided at the Assessment Board
The Assessment Board must approve each UER before it goes to the Programme Committee
The Assessment Board sets the November deadline for each year's UERs
The Assessment Board chair must countersign the Unit Tutor's reflections on the unit
questions.explanation: Section 3.2.2 explains that the UER includes commentary on the unit statistics, and those statistics are provided at LCC's Assessment Board.
questions.source_excerpt: As the form includes commentary on the unit statistics, which is provided at LCC's Assessment Board.

questions.question: The Academic Board is deliberating on the quality of a programme and asks to see completed Unit Evaluation Reports (UERs). Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is the position?
options: No, as UERs are intended only for the Programme Committee and QESC, not for the Board
Only once the External Examiner has reviewed and formally approved each of the reports
No, as completed UERs remain confidential to the Unit Tutor, teaching team and HoPAM
Yes, completed UERs can be made available at all committee and Board deliberations
questions.explanation: Section 3.2.2 states that completed UERs inform the quality assurance and enhancement process and can be made available at all committee and Board deliberations.
questions.source_excerpt: The completed reports inform the quality assurance and enhancement process and can be made available at all committee and Board deliberations.

questions.question: A Standard Verifier has given feedback on a unit you taught this year. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, where should this feedback be reflected?
options: In the Termly Monitoring Report only, as it needs the PEG's immediate attention
Nowhere in College reports, as it is sent straight to the awarding body instead
In the Unit Evaluation Report, alongside the student feedback and unit statistics
In your annual appraisal, as feedback on your individual teaching performance
questions.explanation: Section 3.2.1 states that the UER should include student feedback and unit statistics, and any feedback from External Examiners/Standard Verifiers.
questions.source_excerpt: The UER should incorporate quantitative and qualitative information including student feedback, unit statistics and comparative figures. They should also include reflections from the Unit Tutor and/or teaching team, any feedback from External Examiners/Standard Verifiers

questions.question: A Course Coordinator's Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) draws on the programme's Unit Evaluation Reports (UERs). Under the Annual Monitoring Policy's reporting cycles, how do the two deadlines relate?
options: UERs are due annually by November, ahead of the PAMR in January
UERs are due in March, after the PAMR has been completed in January
Both are due in January and go together to the Programme Committee
The PAMR is due by November, and the UERs follow in January
questions.explanation: The UER review cycle is annually by November and the PAMR's is annually in January, and the PAMR draws on unit evaluation reports, so UERs come first.
questions.source_excerpt: Review Cycle: Annually, by November ... Unit evaluation reports Student feedback; ... Review Cycle: ... Annually, January ... Author: ... Course Coordinators

questions.question: LCC runs several programmes, one of which has a very small cohort this year. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which programmes need a Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR)?
options: Only programmes above a minimum cohort size set by the Academic Board
Only programmes whose pass rate fell below the College average that year
Only programmes flagged as a concern in Termly Monitoring Reports
Each programme offered by the College, including the small one
questions.explanation: Section 3.3.1 states that a PAMR is produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme offered by the College, with no exception for small cohorts.
questions.source_excerpt: A Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) is a reflective report of the preceding academic year, produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme offered by the College.

questions.question: A Course Coordinator drafting the Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) asks whether students' appeals and complaints and lecturers' peer reviews belong in it. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is correct?
options: They are excluded, as appeals and complaints go only to the Academic Board
They are among the areas from which the PAMR draws its information
They are excluded, as peer reviews are confidential staff development records
Appeals and complaints are included, but peer reviews belong in the UER instead
questions.explanation: Section 3.3.1 lists both lecturers' peer review and students' appeals and complaints among the areas the PAMR draws information from.
questions.source_excerpt: This report contains information drawn from the following areas: ... Lecturers' peer review; Minutes of programme committee meeting; Learning resources; Students' appeals and complaints;

questions.question: Pearson asks LCC for a report as part of its Academic Management Review. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which report is intended for this purpose, if requested?
options: The Programme Annual Monitoring Report
Each unit's Unit Evaluation Report
The Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan
The latest Termly Monitoring Report
questions.explanation: The CAMR reporting arrangement in section 3.4.3 states that the Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan is intended for the Academic Board, College Oversight Board and Pearson Academic Management Review (if requested).
questions.source_excerpt: Output: ... Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan ... Intended for: Academic Board (Approval Body), College Oversight Board and Pearson Academic Management Review (if requested).

questions.question: A colleague describes the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR) as simply a record of the year's statistics. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what should the main outcomes of the CAMR be?
options: Sharing good practice, addressing areas for improvement and planning for future issues
Confirming the year's statistics for submission to the awarding bodies and the OfS
Ranking programmes by pass rate to decide which of them should be discontinued next year
Assessing individual lecturers' performance for the College's annual appraisal cycle
questions.explanation: Section 3.4.1 states that the main outcomes of the CAMR should be to share good practice, identify and address areas for improvement and identify future opportunities or issues that need to be planned for.
questions.source_excerpt: The main outcomes of this report should be to share good practice, identify and address areas for improvement and identify opportunities or issues in the future that need to be planned for.

questions.question: A Student Representative who sits on the Programme Committee asks whether they will see the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR). Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is correct?
options: No, the Programme Committee sees the PAMRs only; the CAMR is shared at All Staff Meetings
No, the CAMR goes only to the Academic Board and the College Oversight Board
Yes, it is shared at Programme Committee Meetings, which Student Representatives attend
Only after the College Oversight Board has published a summary of it on the College website
questions.explanation: Section 3.4.2 states that the CAMR is shared at Programme Committee Meetings, and that the Programme Committee is attended by Student Representatives.
questions.source_excerpt: It is also shared at Programme Committee Meetings and All Staff Meetings. In the interest of operating a transparent monitoring process, both the Academic Board and the Programme Committee are attended by Student Representatives.

questions.question: It is February and the Course Coordinators have completed their Programme Annual Monitoring Reports. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which annual report follows next, and who authors it?
options: The Unit Evaluation Reports in March, by each Unit Tutor on the programme
The CAMR and action plan in March, by the Principal or his/her designated person
The CAMR in March, by the Course Coordinators working jointly with QESC
A second round of PAMRs in March, by the Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring
questions.explanation: The PAMR is due annually in January; the CAMR follows annually in March and is authored by the Principal or his/her designated person, as the Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan.
questions.source_excerpt: Review Cycle: ... Annually, January ... Review Cycle: ... Annually, March ... Author: ... Principal or his/her designated person ... Output: ... Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan

questions.question: A Course Coordinator wants to write this year's programme monitoring report in a free format of their own design, because the programme is unusual. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is the position?
options: A free format is acceptable if the HoPAM agrees the programme is too unusual to fit the template
The set template applies, so data can be cross-compared and the overall College collective report built
A free format is acceptable provided the report remains critical, reflective and evidence-based
A free format is acceptable once the External Examiner has endorsed the proposed report structure
questions.explanation: Section 2.3 states that Course Coordinators construct reports through a set template so that data can be cross-compared, enabling an overall College collective annual report; the policy makes no provision for a free format.
questions.source_excerpt: Through a set template, Course Coordinators construct reports in a way that allows for cross-comparison of data, thus enabling an overall College collective annual report to be constructed;

questions.question: A Course Coordinator plans to leave student satisfaction indicators out of the programme report, arguing that the College Annual Monitoring Report already covers the student experience. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, is this acceptable?
options: Yes, as satisfaction data belongs only in the Unit Evaluation Reports written by Unit Tutors
Yes, provided the programme report still identifies key actions for the following year
No, as individual programme reports should include student satisfaction indicators
Yes, as satisfaction is reported orally to the PEG each month rather than in annual reports
questions.explanation: Section 2.5 states that individual programme reports should identify key actions for the following year and should include student satisfaction indicators; coverage in the College report does not remove this requirement.
questions.source_excerpt: Individual programme reports should identify key actions to be taken during the following year and should include student satisfaction indicators;

questions.question: This year's programme and College monitoring reports have gone to the Academic Board. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which describes what happens next?
options: The PEG makes recommendations on future development, and the Board tracks the agreed changes
The Board makes recommendations on future development, and the PEG then tracks the agreed changes
The Board makes recommendations, and the College Oversight Board tracks the agreed changes
QESC makes recommendations, and the HoPAM tracks agreed changes through monthly PEG meetings
questions.explanation: Section 2.6 states that the Academic Board considers programme and College reports and makes recommendations as to future development, and section 2.7 gives the PEG the role of tracking and monitoring suggested and agreed changes through the following year.
questions.source_excerpt: Programme and College reports will be considered by the Academic Board which will make recommendations as to future development; ... The Principal's Executive Group (PEG) will track and monitor suggested and agreed changes throughout the following year

questions.question: After an excellent year, a Course Coordinator proposes that the Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) should record only good practice. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is the position?
options: Acceptable, as areas for improvement are recorded only when a programme has underperformed
Acceptable, provided any improvement areas are raised orally with the PEG at its next meeting
Not acceptable, as the reports should indicate items needing improvement as well as good practice
Acceptable, as improvement areas are identified by the Academic Board rather than in the PAMR
questions.explanation: Section 2.4 requires monitoring reports to indicate good practice as well as items that require improvement, and section 3.3.1 lists both good practices and areas for improvement among the PAMR's contents.
questions.source_excerpt: Annual monitoring reports should be reflective and evidence-based and indicate areas of good practice as well as items that require improvement. ... Students' appeals and complaints; Good practices; Areas for improvements;

questions.question: A new Programme Leader assumes that, because the HoPAM gives an oral report on programmes at every PEG meeting, they need not report anything in writing. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is correct?
options: They are right, as the HoPAM's oral report replaces written reporting by Programme Leaders
They need submit a written report only when the HoPAM requests one on the PEG's behalf
They must instead give their own oral report at each monthly PEG meeting alongside the HoPAM
They must still complete the written Termly Monitoring Report each term, per the template
questions.explanation: The HoPAM's oral report at each PEG meeting (3.1.3) sits alongside, not instead of, the written reporting in 3.1.1-3.1.2: Programme Leaders must complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template.
questions.source_excerpt: written reports are submitted each term. ... Programme Leaders are required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template, ... The HoPAM provides oversight of programmes through an oral report at each PEG meeting

questions.question: A Programme Leader identifies two issues: one needs the PEG's immediate attention, the other is a future issue the College will need to plan for. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which reports are designed to address each?
options: Immediate: the College Annual Monitoring Report; future: the Termly Monitoring Report
Immediate: the Termly Monitoring Report; future: the Unit Evaluation Report
Immediate: the Termly Monitoring Report; future: the College Annual Monitoring Report
Immediate: the Programme Annual Monitoring Report; future: the Unit Evaluation Report
questions.explanation: The Termly Monitoring Report template is designed to highlight to the PEG matters requiring immediate attention (3.1.2), while a main outcome of the CAMR is to identify future opportunities or issues that need to be planned for (3.4.1).
questions.source_excerpt: the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template, which is designed to highlight to the PEG any matters that require their immediate attention; ... The main outcomes of this report should be to share good practice, identify and address areas for improvement and identify opportunities or issues in the future that need to be planned for.

questions.question: A unit is taught by its Unit Tutor together with two other lecturers. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, how should the Unit Evaluation Report (UER) for that unit be produced?
options: The Unit Tutor completes it, including reflections from the Unit Tutor and/or the teaching team
Each lecturer completes a separate UER, and the Course Coordinator merges them into the PAMR
The Course Coordinator completes it after collecting reflections from all three lecturers
The most senior lecturer completes it, and the Unit Tutor adds the student feedback section
questions.explanation: Section 3.2.1 states that the standard UER is for completion by the Unit Tutor and should include reflections from the Unit Tutor and/or teaching team.
questions.source_excerpt: LCC uses a standard Unit Evaluation Report (UER) across its taught provision, for completion by the Unit Tutor. ... They should also include reflections from the Unit Tutor and/or teaching team,

questions.question: A unit is delivered twice in the same academic year, to two separate intakes. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, how many Unit Evaluation Reports (UERs) should be completed for that unit?
options: One combined UER covering both intakes, submitted by the November deadline
Two, as a UER should be completed after each instance of unit delivery
One, covering whichever intake had the larger number of enrolled students
Two, but only where the two intakes' pass rates differ by a significant margin
questions.explanation: Section 3.2.2 requires a UER after each instance of Unit delivery, so two deliveries need two reports; the policy makes no provision for combining them.
questions.source_excerpt: A Unit Evaluation Report should be completed after each instance of Unit delivery.

questions.question: A Unit Tutor on a newly introduced optional unit wants to design their own evaluation form instead of using the Unit Evaluation Report (UER). Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what applies?
options: LCC uses a standard UER across its taught provision, so the standard form applies
A bespoke form is allowed for new units until their first Assessment Board has met
A bespoke form is allowed if the Programme Committee and QESC approve it in advance
Optional units are covered by the PAMR instead, so no evaluation form is needed
questions.explanation: Section 3.2.1 states that LCC uses a standard Unit Evaluation Report across its taught provision, and 3.2.2 requires one after each instance of Unit delivery; there is no exception for new or optional units.
questions.source_excerpt: LCC uses a standard Unit Evaluation Report (UER) across its taught provision, for completion by the Unit Tutor. ... A Unit Evaluation Report should be completed after each instance of Unit delivery.

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which of the following is not listed among the areas a Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) draws its information from?
options: Unit evaluation reports, student feedback and learning resources
Information on application, admission, induction, retention and dropout
Minutes of the programme committee meeting and lecturers' peer review
Records of lecturers' continuing professional development activity
questions.explanation: Section 3.3.1 lists unit evaluation reports, student feedback, learning resources, application to dropout data, programme committee minutes and lecturers' peer review, but not lecturers' continuing professional development records.
questions.source_excerpt: This report contains information drawn from the following areas: ... Information on application, admission, induction, retention and dropout; ... Unit evaluation reports Student feedback; Lecturers' peer review; Minutes of programme committee meeting; Learning resources;

questions.question: A Course Coordinator's draft Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) uses the pass rate as its only measure of academic performance. Which other quantitative measures does the Annual Monitoring Policy give as examples?
options: Completion rate and achievement rate
Attendance rate and submission rate
Employment rate and further study rate
Student-staff ratio and contact hours
questions.explanation: Section 3.3.1 gives pass rate, completion rate and achievement rate as examples of quantitative information on academic performance in the PAMR.
questions.source_excerpt: Quantitative information on academic performance (eg. pass rate, completion rate and achievement rate);

questions.question: A programme had no External Examiner report in the preceding academic year. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, how does this affect its Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR)?
options: The PAMR must be postponed until that year's External Examiner report has been obtained
The programme is excluded from annual monitoring until an External Examiner is appointed
The PAMR goes ahead only once the Principal has commissioned an external review instead
The PAMR is still produced, as external examiner reports are drawn on wherever applicable
questions.explanation: A PAMR is produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme, and external examiner reports are included only wherever applicable, so the report still goes ahead.
questions.source_excerpt: produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme offered by the College. ... External examiner reports wherever applicable (considering quality and standards);

questions.question: Student feedback on a unit can feed into the UER, then the Programme Annual Monitoring Report, then the College Annual Monitoring Report. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, who authors each report, in that order?
options: Unit Tutor; Course Coordinators; the Principal or his/her designated person
Unit Tutor; Programme Leaders; the Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring
Course Coordinators; the Unit Tutor; the Principal or his/her designated person
Programme Leaders; Course Coordinators; the Academic Board as the approval body
questions.explanation: The reporting arrangements name the Unit Tutor as author of the UER, the Course Coordinators as author of the PAMR, and the Principal or his/her designated person as author of the CAMR.
questions.source_excerpt: for completion by the Unit Tutor. ... Author: ... Course Coordinators ... Output: ... Programme Annual Monitoring Report ... Author: ... Principal or his/her designated person ... Output: ... Annual CAMR Report and Action Plan

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy's reporting arrangements, which statement about the intended audiences of the Unit Evaluation Report (UER) and the Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR) is correct?
options: Both go to the PEG, which signs them off before the College report is written
Both are for the Programme Committee and QESC; only the PAMR adds the External Examiner
The UER is intended for the Programme Committee only, while the PAMR goes only to QESC
Both are intended for the College Oversight Board, while QESC receives only the CAMR
questions.explanation: The UER is intended for the Programme Committee and QESC; the PAMR is intended for the Programme Committee, QESC and the External Examiner (if requested).
questions.source_excerpt: Intended for: Programme Committee and QESC ... Intended for: Programme Committee, QESC and External Examiner (if requested)

questions.question: A colleague states that the College Oversight Board approves the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR). Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which statement is accurate?
options: The PEG approves the CAMR, and the Academic Board and Oversight Board then receive it
The College Oversight Board approves it once the Academic Board has recommended it
QESC approves the CAMR, and the College Oversight Board receives it for information
The Academic Board approves the CAMR, and the College Oversight Board receives it
questions.explanation: Section 3.4.2 states that the CAMR is approved by the Academic Board and received by the College Oversight Board; the reporting arrangement names the Academic Board as the Approval Body.
questions.source_excerpt: The CAMR is approved by the Academic Board and is received by the College Oversight Board. ... Intended for: Academic Board (Approval Body), College Oversight Board

questions.question: A draft College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR) reflects on the academic standards students achieved but not on whether those standards remain up to date. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what should be added?
options: A comparison with competitor colleges' standards on equivalent programmes
Written confirmation from each awarding body that its standards are reapproved
Reflection on the continuing currency and relevance of the standards achieved
Each External Examiner's full report, appended to the CAMR as an annex
questions.explanation: Section 3.4.1 states that the CAMR reflects on the academic standards achieved and their continuing currency and relevance.
questions.source_excerpt: The CAMR reflects on the learning opportunities students have experienced, the academic standards achieved, and their continuing currency and relevance.

questions.question: A Course Coordinator is preparing the student profile section of a Programme Annual Monitoring Report (PAMR). Which details does the Annual Monitoring Policy specify as student profile information?
options: Gender, age and prior entry qualification
Gender, nationality and entry qualification
Nationality, ethnicity and home language
Age, disability status and entry route
questions.explanation: Section 3.3.1 lists student profile information in the PAMR as gender, nationality and entry qualification.
questions.source_excerpt: Student profile information (gender, nationality, entry qualification);

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, you are both Programme Leader and Course Coordinator for one programme, and you teach none of its units. Which monitoring reports are you responsible for authoring?
options: The Termly Monitoring Report only, as the HoPAM writes the programme's annual report
The Programme Annual Monitoring Report only, as the HoPAM reports termly on your behalf
The Programme Annual Monitoring Report and the Unit Evaluation Reports for its units
The Termly Monitoring Report each term and the Programme Annual Monitoring Report
questions.explanation: Programme Leaders complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term (3.1.2) and Course Coordinators author the PAMR (3.3.2); UERs are completed by the Unit Tutor (3.2.1), so they are not yours.
questions.source_excerpt: Programme Leaders are required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template ... for completion by the Unit Tutor. ... Author: ... Course Coordinators ... Output: ... Programme Annual Monitoring Report

questions.question: Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, the PEG meets three times during one term. Over that term, how many oral reports should the HoPAM give, and how many Termly Monitoring Reports should each Programme Leader complete?
options: Three oral reports from the HoPAM, and one Termly Monitoring Report from each Programme Leader
One oral report from the HoPAM, and three Termly Monitoring Reports from each Programme Leader
Three oral reports from the HoPAM, and three Termly Monitoring Reports from each Programme Leader
One oral report from the HoPAM, and one Termly Monitoring Report from each Programme Leader
questions.explanation: The HoPAM gives an oral report at each PEG meeting (3.1.3), so three meetings mean three oral reports, while each Programme Leader completes the Termly Monitoring Report once per term (3.1.2).
questions.source_excerpt: Programme Leaders are required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template ... The HoPAM provides oversight of programmes through an oral report at each PEG meeting, which typically takes place once per month.

questions.question: The Principal designates the Head of Programmes and Academic Monitoring (HoPAM) to write this year's College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR). Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, which statement is correct?
options: The HoPAM may write it, but the College Oversight Board then becomes its approval body instead
The HoPAM cannot write it, as the CAMR must be authored by the Principal personally
The HoPAM cannot write it, as the CAMR is compiled jointly by the Course Coordinators from their PAMRs
The HoPAM may write it as the Principal's designated person, and the Academic Board still approves it
questions.explanation: The CAMR's author is the Principal or his/her designated person, so a designated HoPAM may write it; the CAMR is still approved by the Academic Board and only received by the College Oversight Board.
questions.source_excerpt: The CAMR is approved by the Academic Board and is received by the College Oversight Board. ... Author: ... Principal or his/her designated person ... Intended for: Academic Board (Approval Body), College Oversight Board

questions.question: The Academic Board has suggested a change to a programme but has not yet agreed it. A colleague says the Principal's Executive Group (PEG) will only begin monitoring the change once it is agreed. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, what is correct?
options: The PEG tracks and monitors suggested as well as agreed changes throughout the following year
The colleague is right; suggested changes remain with the Academic Board until they are formally agreed
Suggested changes are monitored by the HoPAM through Termly Monitoring Reports until agreed
Suggested changes go into the next CAMR action plan and are not tracked in the meantime
questions.explanation: Section 2.7 states that the PEG will track and monitor suggested and agreed changes throughout the following year, so monitoring does not wait for a change to be agreed.
questions.source_excerpt: The Principal's Executive Group (PEG) will track and monitor suggested and agreed changes throughout the following year and report back to the Academic Board at such times as the Board may require.

questions.question: Over an academic year of three terms, a programme with one Programme Leader delivers each of its six units once. Under the Annual Monitoring Policy, how many Termly Monitoring Reports, Unit Evaluation Reports (UERs) and Programme Annual Monitoring Reports (PAMRs) are due for it?
options: One Termly Monitoring Report, six UERs and three PAMRs
Three Termly Monitoring Reports, one UER and one PAMR
Three Termly Monitoring Reports, six UERs and one PAMR
Three Termly Monitoring Reports, six UERs and three PAMRs
questions.explanation: Programme Leaders complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term (three), a UER is completed after each instance of unit delivery (six), and a PAMR is produced at the end of each academic year for each programme (one).
questions.source_excerpt: Programme Leaders are required to complete the Termly Monitoring Report once per term according to the template ... A Unit Evaluation Report should be completed after each instance of Unit delivery. ... produced at the end of each academic year for each Programme offered by the College.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, a supplier bidding for a College contract offers you a cash payment to favour their bid. What must you do?
options: Refuse it and mention the approach at your next annual appraisal meeting
Refuse the payment and report it immediately to the Registrar
Accept it, then record it in the gifts register by the end of the month
Refuse it; no report is needed as no money changed hands
questions.explanation: The policy states that an offered or solicited bribe must be refused (unless personal safety is at risk) and reported immediately to the Registrar.
questions.source_excerpt: If a bribe is offered or solicited, it must be refused unless personal safety is at risk and reported immediately to the Registrar.

questions.question: A supplier sends you a £25 gift card, usable like cash in most shops, to thank you for your help on a project. How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy treat this?
options: It is acceptable, as the value is modest and proportionate to the help given
It may be kept once the Registrar has entered it in the gifts register
It is not allowed, as cash-equivalent gifts are strictly prohibited
It may be kept if its cash value is shared equally among your team
questions.explanation: A gift card that can be spent like cash is a cash-equivalent gift, and the policy strictly prohibits cash or cash-equivalent gifts.
questions.source_excerpt: Cash or cash-equivalent gifts are strictly prohibited

questions.question: A partner organisation invites you to a dinner, hosted by them, to discuss a collaboration. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what must happen before you accept?
options: Nothing, as hospitality with the host present needs no approval
You must declare it to the Registrar within 30 days after the event
Your line manager must approve it verbally on the day
The Principal must authorise the hospitality in advance
questions.explanation: The policy requires all gifts and hospitality to be authorised in advance by the Principal.
questions.source_excerpt: All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, how may a staff member's failure to report bribery concerns be treated?
options: It is acceptable if the staff member was not directly involved
It becomes a breach once the sum involved exceeds a set threshold
It may in itself be treated as a breach of this policy
It is a matter for the staff member's own discretion
questions.explanation: The policy states that failing to report concerns may itself be treated as a breach of the policy, and suspected bribery must be reported even by staff who are not directly involved.
questions.source_excerpt: Suspected bribery must also be reported promptly, even if the individual is not directly involved. ... Failure to report concerns may itself be treated as a breach of this policy.

questions.question: Apart from reporting directly to the responsible College officer, which route does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy name for raising concerns about bribery, fraud or corruption?
options: The College's Staff Grievance Procedure
The College's Whistleblowing Policy
The Student Complaints Procedure
The annual staff engagement survey
questions.explanation: The policy requires staff to report suspected or actual fraud, bribery or corruption promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy.
questions.source_excerpt: Staff are required to report any suspected or actual fraud, bribery or corruption promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy.

questions.question: The Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy requires an offered or solicited bribe to be refused, with one exception. What is that exception?
options: Where the offer is below the College's gift threshold
Where the offer comes from a long-standing partner
Where the offer is made by a senior member of College staff
Where refusing would put your personal safety at risk
questions.explanation: The only exception the policy gives to refusing a bribe is where personal safety is at risk; the bribe must still be reported immediately to the Registrar.
questions.source_excerpt: If a bribe is offered or solicited, it must be refused unless personal safety is at risk and reported immediately to the Registrar.

questions.question: A contractor gives you two free concert tickets; nobody from the contractor will attend with you. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, how is this treated?
options: As a gift, because hospitality without a host present is treated as a gift
As hospitality, which needs no authorisation if it is outside working hours
As a private matter that falls outside the scope of the policy
As a business expense to be declared through the payroll system
questions.explanation: The policy states that hospitality without a host present is treated as a gift, so the gifts rules (including advance authorisation by the Principal) apply.
questions.source_excerpt: Hospitality without a host present is treated as a gift.

questions.question: An overseas recruitment agent suggests the College pays a 'consultancy fee' to a third party so that a foreign official approves a partnership faster. What does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy say?
options: It is permitted if the fee is routed through the agent, not the College
It is prohibited, as bribery is banned whether direct or indirect
It is permitted if the fee is reasonable and proportionate
It is permitted if the Principal authorises it in advance
questions.explanation: The policy strictly prohibits bribery directly or indirectly, expressly including improperly influencing foreign public officials and making payments to third parties for improper benefit.
questions.source_excerpt: At LCC it is strictly prohibited for any employee or person acting for or on behalf of the College to engage in bribery, fraud or corrupt practices, directly or indirectly. This includes: ... b) Improperly influencing foreign public officials c) Making payments to third parties for improper benefit

questions.question: How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy define corruption?
options: The misuse of entrusted power or position for private gain
Any failure to follow the College's financial procedures
The accidental mishandling of College funds or assets
The acceptance of any gift from a supplier, whatever its value
questions.explanation: The policy defines corruption as the misuse of entrusted power or position for private gain.
questions.source_excerpt: Corruption is the misuse of entrusted power or position for private gain

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which of the following is a criminal offence under the Bribery Act 2010?
options: Accepting authorised hospitality from a College partner
Failing to complete anti-bribery training on time
Raising a bribery concern that later proves to be unfounded
A commercial organisation failing to prevent bribery
questions.explanation: The policy lists four offences under the Bribery Act 2010, including a commercial organisation failing to prevent bribery.
questions.source_excerpt: Under the Bribery Act 2010, it is a criminal offence to: ... d) as a commercial organisation, to fail to prevent bribery

questions.question: To whom does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy apply?
options: Senior managers and budget holders, with junior and support staff exempt
Permanent employees on College contracts, but not agency or self-employed workers
All employees of any role or level, and anyone working on the College's behalf
Staff in finance, admissions and partnerships, with other departments exempt
questions.explanation: The policy applies to all employees regardless of role or seniority and extends to anyone working for or on the College's behalf, such as self-employed individuals and agency workers.
questions.source_excerpt: This policy applies to all employees of London Churchill College, regardless of role or seniority. It also extends to anyone working for or on our behalf (e.g., self-employed individuals, agency workers).

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what is the maximum penalty an individual found guilty of bribery under the Bribery Act 2010 may face?
options: Up to 10 years in prison and/or an unlimited fine
Up to 2 years in prison and/or a £5,000 fine
Up to 5 years in prison, with no financial penalty
An unlimited fine, as bribery is not an imprisonable offence
questions.explanation: The policy warns that individuals found guilty of bribery under the Bribery Act 2010 may face up to 10 years in prison and/or an unlimited fine.
questions.source_excerpt: if they are found guilty by a court of committing bribery under the Bribery Act 2010, they may face up to 10 years in prison and/or an unlimited fine.

questions.question: The Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy defines bribery as offering or accepting any gift, loan, payment, reward or advantage for personal gain as an encouragement to do what?
options: Something which falls outside the person's normal job duties
Something which the person has not been trained to do
Something which is dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust
Something which has not been approved by their line manager
questions.explanation: The policy defines bribery as offering or accepting an advantage for personal gain as an encouragement to do something dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust.
questions.source_excerpt: the offering or accepting of any gift, loan, payment, reward or advantage for personal gain as an encouragement to do something which is dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust.

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what attitude does the College take towards corrupt activities of any kind?
options: Zero tolerance, whether committed by College employees or by third parties acting for it
Zero tolerance for employees, with third parties bound only by their own codes
Case-by-case tolerance, depending on the value involved and the intent behind it
Zero tolerance for serious cases, with minor ones resolved by line managers
questions.explanation: The policy states a zero-tolerance attitude to corrupt activities of any kind, whether committed by College employees or by third parties acting for or on behalf of the College.
questions.source_excerpt: there is a zero-tolerance attitude towards corrupt activities of any kind, whether committed by College employees or by third parties acting for or on behalf of London Churchill College.

questions.question: Besides offering or accepting a bribe, the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy lists bribing which type of person as a separate criminal offence under the Bribery Act 2010?
options: A College external auditor
A foreign public official
An awarding body examiner
A student's financial sponsor
questions.explanation: The policy lists bribing a foreign public official as one of the criminal offences under the Bribery Act 2010, alongside giving and accepting bribes.
questions.source_excerpt: Under the Bribery Act 2010, it is a criminal offence to: ... c) bribe a foreign public official;

questions.question: Besides the penalties faced by individuals, what does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy say the College itself may face where bribery occurs?
options: A fine only, as organisations cannot be prosecuted
No penalty, as only individuals can be prosecuted
An internal review led by the Registrar only
Prosecution and liability to pay a fine
questions.explanation: The policy warns that, as well as individuals being convicted, the College may also face prosecution and be liable to pay a fine.
questions.source_excerpt: The College may also face prosecution and be liable to pay a fine.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy's definition, what can the advantage offered or given in a bribe consist of?
options: Cash payments only, over a set monetary value
Money, gifts, hospitality or anything of value
Money or physical gifts, but not hospitality
Payments made through a third party only
questions.explanation: The policy describes bribery as a form of corruption involving money, gifts, hospitality or anything of value as an inducement or reward for dishonest or illegal conduct.
questions.source_excerpt: It is a form of corruption involving money, gifts, hospitality, or anything of value as an inducement or reward for dishonest or illegal conduct.

questions.question: What does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy say about applying it when the College engages third parties such as suppliers and contractors?
options: It must not be applied, as they follow their own policies
It applies only to contractors working on College premises
The College encourages its application to them
It applies only once a contract exceeds a set value
questions.explanation: The policy states that the College encourages the application of the policy when engaging third parties, including suppliers and contractors.
questions.source_excerpt: The College encourages the application of this policy when engaging third parties including suppliers and contractors.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which of these measures does the College commit to in relation to third parties?
options: Unannounced inspections of their premises
Annual criminal record checks on their staff
Mandatory anti-bribery training for their staff
Due diligence on the organisations it engages
questions.explanation: Among the measures the College commits to, the policy lists conducting due diligence on third parties.
questions.source_excerpt: The College will: a) Conduct due diligence on third parties

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what disciplinary action may the College take for breaches, where appropriate?
options: Action including dismissal or termination of contracts
A written warning at most, issued by a line manager
Suspension without pay, but never outright dismissal
No internal action, as the police handle all cases
questions.explanation: The policy states the College will take disciplinary action where appropriate, including dismissal or termination of contracts.
questions.source_excerpt: d) Take disciplinary action where appropriate, including dismissal or termination of contracts

questions.question: The Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy recognises that reasonable and proportionate gifts and hospitality may support positive relationships. On what condition?
options: Where the giver is an established College partner
Where nothing is expected in return
Where the value is below £50 per item
Where they are shared with the whole team
questions.explanation: The policy accepts that reasonable and proportionate gifts and hospitality may support positive relationships only where nothing is expected in return.
questions.source_excerpt: The College recognises that reasonable and proportionate gifts and hospitality may support positive relationships where nothing is expected in return.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, who maintains the register of approved gifts and hospitality?
options: The Principal
The Registrar
The Head of Finance
The Human Resources team
questions.explanation: The policy states that the Registrar maintains a register of approved items; the Principal authorises gifts and hospitality in advance.
questions.source_excerpt: The Registrar maintains a register of approved items

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, all gifts and hospitality arrangements must meet which requirements?
options: Confidential, modest and reported once a year
Approved afterwards by a line manager and logged
Transparent, reasonable and accurately recorded
Kept below a fixed value and shared with the team
questions.explanation: The policy requires all gifts and hospitality arrangements to be transparent, reasonable and accurately recorded.
questions.source_excerpt: All arrangements must be transparent, reasonable, and accurately recorded.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, how often does the College assess fraud risks across its operations?
options: At least annually, and in response to material changes
Every three years, as part of the scheduled policy review
Only after a suspected fraud has been reported to it
Monthly, through each department's own risk register
questions.explanation: The policy states that the College assesses fraud risks at least annually and in response to material changes.
questions.source_excerpt: The College assesses fraud risks at least annually, and in response to material changes, across its operations

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, how will reported concerns about fraud, bribery or corruption be investigated, where appropriate?
options: Publicly, so lessons can be shared College-wide
Informally, by the staff member's line manager
Only after several reports have been received
In a timely, proportionate and confidential manner
questions.explanation: The policy states that all concerns will be treated seriously and, where appropriate, investigated in a timely, proportionate and confidential manner.
questions.source_excerpt: All concerns will be treated seriously and, where appropriate, investigated in a timely, proportionate and confidential manner

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what records does the College maintain to support oversight, audit and organisational learning?
options: Records of substantiated cases only, not unproven concerns
Anonymised summaries only, with outcomes not retained
Records of reported concerns, investigations and outcomes
Records of concerns raised through whistleblowing only
questions.explanation: The policy states that records of reported concerns, investigations and outcomes are maintained to support oversight, audit and organisational learning.
questions.source_excerpt: Records of reported concerns, investigations and outcomes are maintained to support oversight, audit and organisational learning.

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which staff receive enhanced training on fraud, bribery and corruption?
options: Staff working in higher-risk roles
Staff who have previously breached this policy
Newly appointed senior managers only
Staff acting as whistleblowing contacts
questions.explanation: The policy's training includes mandatory induction, periodic refreshers and enhanced training for higher-risk roles.
questions.source_excerpt: This includes mandatory induction training, periodic refresher training and enhanced training for higher-risk roles.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, you overhear a colleague agreeing to take money from an applicant's agent to fast-track an offer. You are not involved yourself. What must you do?
options: Report the suspected bribery promptly to the Registrar
Nothing, as only staff directly involved have a duty to report
Wait until you hold documentary proof before telling anyone
Ask the agent to explain before deciding whether to report
questions.explanation: Suspected bribery must be reported promptly even by staff who are not directly involved, and staff report such concerns to the Registrar (or via the Whistleblowing Policy).
questions.source_excerpt: Suspected bribery must also be reported promptly, even if the individual is not directly involved. ... Staff are required to report any suspected or actual fraud, bribery or corruption promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy.

questions.question: A finance colleague suspects a supplier of submitting falsified invoices, which would be fraud rather than bribery. What does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy require the colleague to do?
options: Nothing under this policy, as it deals with bribery rather than fraud
Report it promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy
Report it only once an audit has proven that fraud has taken place
Hold it back until the ARRC next reviews fraud risk and incidents
questions.explanation: The policy's reporting duty covers suspected or actual fraud as well as bribery and corruption, and such concerns go promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy.
questions.source_excerpt: Staff are required to report any suspected or actual fraud, bribery or corruption promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy.

questions.question: A staff member asks an applicant for £200 to speed up an offer letter. The applicant refuses and no money changes hands. How do the Bribery Act 2010 offences listed in the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy apply?
options: No offence arises, because no money was ever handed over
An offence arises only if the letter is issued early
Requesting a bribe is a criminal offence in its own right
It is a disciplinary matter for the College, not a crime
questions.explanation: The policy lists requesting a bribe as a criminal offence under the Bribery Act 2010, alongside agreeing to receive or accepting one, so no payment is needed for the offence.
questions.source_excerpt: Under the Bribery Act 2010, it is a criminal offence to: a) offer, promise or give a bribe; b) request, agree to receive or accept a bribe;

questions.question: A visiting partner offers you a modest gift. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which describes the correct process for accepting it?
options: The Registrar authorises it in advance; the Principal records it on the register
You accept it, then the Registrar records it on the register within a month
Your line manager authorises it in advance; HR records it on the register
The Principal authorises it in advance; the Registrar records it on the register
questions.explanation: All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal, and the Registrar maintains the register of approved items.
questions.source_excerpt: All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal ... The Registrar maintains a register of approved items

questions.question: The Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy divides responsibility for the College's counter-fraud framework between the Principal, the Registrar and the ARRC. Which split is correct?
options: Registrar: overall responsibility; Principal: operational oversight; ARRC: scrutiny
Principal: overall responsibility; ARRC: operational oversight; Registrar: scrutiny
ARRC: overall responsibility; Principal: operational oversight; Registrar: scrutiny
Principal: overall responsibility; Registrar: operational oversight; ARRC: scrutiny
questions.explanation: Overall responsibility rests with the Principal, operational oversight is delegated to the Registrar, and the ARRC provides scrutiny.
questions.source_excerpt: Overall responsibility for the implementation and effectiveness of this framework rests with the Principal, with operational oversight delegated to the Registrar and scrutiny provided by the ARRC.

questions.question: Midway through the year, the College starts recruiting through a new overseas partnership, a material change to its operations. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, when should the related fraud risks be assessed?
options: In response to the change, without waiting for the next annual assessment
At the next annual assessment, as mid-year reassessments are not required
Only once a suspected fraud involving the new partnership has been reported
At the next three-yearly policy review, when every risk is reassessed together
questions.explanation: The College assesses fraud risks at least annually and also in response to material changes, across operations including partnerships.
questions.source_excerpt: The College assesses fraud risks at least annually, and in response to material changes, across its operations, including finance, procurement, admissions and partnerships.

questions.question: A finance officer is able to both raise and approve the same supplier payments. Which internal control named in the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy does this arrangement lack?
options: Mandatory job rotation
Annual staff vetting
Segregation of duties
Clear-desk procedures
questions.explanation: Letting one person both raise and approve a payment removes segregation of duties, which the policy names among its proportionate internal controls against fraud.
questions.source_excerpt: Proportionate internal controls, including segregation of duties, approval processes, reconciliations and due diligence are implemented to mitigate identified risks and ensure transparency and accountability.

questions.question: A lecturer has repeatedly failed to complete the periodic refresher training on fraud, bribery and corruption. What does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy say about this?
options: Refresher training is optional once induction training is complete
Completion is monitored and recorded, and non-compliance is followed up
It matters only for higher-risk roles, so no action needs to be taken
Missing the training leads to automatic dismissal from the College
questions.explanation: All staff receive periodic refresher training, and the policy states that training completion is monitored and recorded, with non-compliance followed up appropriately.
questions.source_excerpt: This includes mandatory induction training, periodic refresher training and enhanced training for higher-risk roles. Training completion is monitored and recorded, and non-compliance is followed up appropriately.

questions.question: An agency worker placed in the admissions team is offered money by an applicant's family to overlook missing documents. How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy apply to the worker?
options: It does not apply, as only the agency's own code covers agency staff
It applies, as it extends to anyone working for or on the College's behalf
It applies only once the worker has been in post for more than three months
It applies only if the worker has completed the College's induction training
questions.explanation: The policy applies to all employees and extends to anyone working for or on the College's behalf, expressly including agency workers.
questions.source_excerpt: This policy applies to all employees of London Churchill College, regardless of role or seniority. It also extends to anyone working for or on our behalf (e.g., self-employed individuals, agency workers).

questions.question: An investigation under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy finds evidence that a staff member has committed a criminal bribery offence. Besides internal action, what does the policy say the College will do where necessary?
options: Refer the matter to external authorities
Settle it internally to protect its reputation
Close the case once the money has been repaid
Wait for the ARRC's next annual report to act
questions.explanation: The College commits to referring matters to external authorities where necessary, and investigations escalate to external authorities where necessary.
questions.source_excerpt: Refer matters to external authorities where necessary ... investigated in a timely, proportionate and confidential manner, with escalation to external authorities where necessary.

questions.question: Just before a tender decision, a bidding supplier sends you a modest bottle of wine with a note saying they 'look forward to your support'. Why does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy NOT treat this as an acceptable gift?
options: Because alcohol is banned outright under the gifts and hospitality rules
Because supplier gifts must be worth under £20 to be accepted by staff
Because gifts are acceptable only where nothing is expected in return
Because gifts must be shared with the whole team, not kept by one person
questions.explanation: The policy accepts reasonable and proportionate gifts only where nothing is expected in return; a gift tied to hoped-for support in a tender fails that test.
questions.source_excerpt: The College recognises that reasonable and proportionate gifts and hospitality may support positive relationships where nothing is expected in return.

questions.question: A company bidding for a College contract offers the College a large donation. Which of these is a commitment the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy makes that applies to the donation?
options: Accepting donations from bidders only after the contract is awarded
Keeping donations confidential so they cannot influence the tender
Returning any donation received from a current or potential supplier
Ensuring transparency in transactions, donations and partnerships
questions.explanation: Among its measures, the College commits to ensuring transparency in transactions, donations and partnerships.
questions.source_excerpt: Ensure transparency in transactions, donations, and partnerships

questions.question: According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, how is oversight of fraud risk, incidents and the effectiveness of controls arranged?
options: Senior management and committees such as ARRC, with at least annual reporting
The Registrar alone, reporting to the Board of Directors every three years
Each department for its own area, with no central reporting required
External auditors, reporting to the College only when a fraud is found
questions.explanation: Senior management and relevant committees, including ARRC, oversee fraud risk, incidents and controls, supported by periodic reporting at least annually.
questions.source_excerpt: Senior management and relevant committees, including ARRC, oversee fraud risk, incidents and the effectiveness of controls. Periodic reporting (at least annually) supports appropriate scrutiny, governance and continuous improvement.

questions.question: An internal audit finds a weakness in how procurement approvals are recorded. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, how should the lessons learned be used?
options: Only to decide whether disciplinary action should be taken against staff
To strengthen controls and inform improvements to training and guidance
Kept within the audit team and not shared, to protect confidentiality
Held over until the policy's next scheduled review before any change
questions.explanation: The policy states that lessons learned from incidents, audits and risk reviews are used to strengthen controls and inform ongoing improvements to training and guidance.
questions.source_excerpt: Lessons learned from incidents, audits and risk reviews are used to strengthen controls and inform ongoing improvements to training and guidance.

questions.question: After you quietly let a supplier's tender through past the deadline, the supplier sends you £100 'as a thank you'. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy's definition, can this be bribery even though it came afterwards?
options: No, a bribe must be offered before the act it is meant to influence
No, a payment after the event is a gift for the Registrar to record
Yes, bribery covers a reward for dishonest conduct, not only an inducement
Only if the amount exceeds the College's limit for gifts from suppliers
questions.explanation: The policy defines bribery as involving anything of value given as an inducement or a reward for dishonest or illegal conduct, so a payment after the event can still be a bribe.
questions.source_excerpt: It is a form of corruption involving money, gifts, hospitality, or anything of value as an inducement or reward for dishonest or illegal conduct.

questions.question: On a recruitment trip, a College officer is threatened with harm unless they pay an official, and pays because their personal safety is at risk. What does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy still require of the officer?
options: Nothing further, as the safety exception covers the whole of the incident
An entry in the gifts and hospitality register kept by the Registrar
An immediate report of the incident and the payment to the Registrar
Written approval from the Principal before the officer travels home
questions.explanation: The personal-safety exception relieves the officer only of the duty to refuse; the policy still requires the bribe to be reported immediately to the Registrar.
questions.source_excerpt: If a bribe is offered or solicited, it must be refused unless personal safety is at risk and reported immediately to the Registrar.

questions.question: Overseas, a foreign official asks a College recruitment officer for a small unofficial 'processing fee' to release student documents, saying it is local custom. Nobody is under any threat. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what must the officer do?
options: Refuse it and report it, as only a risk to personal safety permits otherwise
Pay it, as small customary payments made abroad fall outside the policy
Pay it, provided the Principal authorises it in advance as hospitality
Refuse it, and report it only if the official asks for it a second time
questions.explanation: A solicited bribe must be refused and reported immediately to the Registrar; the only exception the policy allows is a risk to personal safety, and improperly influencing foreign public officials is expressly prohibited.
questions.source_excerpt: Improperly influencing foreign public officials ... If a bribe is offered or solicited, it must be refused unless personal safety is at risk and reported immediately to the Registrar.

questions.question: Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which of these offers could NOT be accepted, even if the Principal were asked to authorise it in advance?
options: A modest book offered by a partner university, with nothing expected in return
A hosted working lunch with a partner organisation to discuss a collaboration
Tickets to a local theatre from a contractor, who will not attend with you
A £50 cash payment tucked into a thank-you card from a satisfied supplier
questions.explanation: Cash or cash-equivalent gifts are strictly prohibited, so advance authorisation cannot make them acceptable; other reasonable gifts and hospitality may be accepted once the Principal authorises them in advance.
questions.source_excerpt: Cash or cash-equivalent gifts are strictly prohibited ... All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal

questions.question: A lecturer accepts a modest gift from a visiting partner without asking anyone, then asks the Registrar to add it to the register of approved items. What does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy say about this?
options: The register entry approves the gift, as the Registrar keeps the register
The gift needed the Principal's authorisation before it was accepted
The gift complies as long as it is registered within a month of receipt
Modest partner gifts need only be recorded, not authorised by anyone
questions.explanation: All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal; the Registrar only maintains the register of items already approved, so a later register entry does not cure the lack of authorisation.
questions.source_excerpt: All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal ... The Registrar maintains a register of approved items

questions.question: A manager enrolled on a College course uses their authority to waive their own tuition fee without justification. Nobody offers, requests or receives anything from anyone else. Which definition in the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy does this conduct meet?
options: Neither definition, as no advantage passed between two separate parties
Neither definition, as a staff member's own fees fall outside the policy
Corruption, as a misuse of entrusted power or position for private gain
Bribery, as the fee waiver is a gift the manager has given themselves
questions.explanation: The policy defines corruption as the misuse of entrusted power or position for private gain, which needs no exchange; bribery, by contrast, involves offering, giving, requesting or accepting an advantage.
questions.source_excerpt: Corruption is the misuse of entrusted power or position for private gain

questions.question: The College engages (a) a self-employed recruitment agent to work on its behalf and (b) a company that supplies its stationery. How does the scope of the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy treat each of them?
options: It applies to both, as a binding condition of every College contract
