It applies to neither, as neither of them is a College employee
It applies to the supplier, with its use by the agent encouraged
It applies to the agent, with its use by the supplier encouraged
questions.explanation: The policy extends to anyone working for or on the College's behalf, such as self-employed individuals, while for third parties such as suppliers the College only encourages its application.
questions.source_excerpt: It also extends to anyone working for or on our behalf (e.g., self-employed individuals, agency workers). ... The College encourages the application of this policy when engaging third parties including suppliers and contractors.

questions.question: A recruitment agent acting for the College pays a bribe to win student referrals, and no College staff member knew about it. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, could the College itself face criminal consequences?
options: Yes, it may face prosecution and a fine for failing to prevent bribery
No, only the individual who actually paid the bribe can be prosecuted
No, as the agent is an outside third party, not a College employee
Yes, but only if a College employee knew of or approved the payment
questions.explanation: Failing to prevent bribery is a criminal offence for a commercial organisation under the Bribery Act 2010, and the policy warns that the College may face prosecution and a fine.
questions.source_excerpt: d) as a commercial organisation, to fail to prevent bribery ... The College may also face prosecution and be liable to pay a fine.

questions.question: An employee is convicted in court of accepting bribes from a College supplier. Taken together, which consequences for the employee does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy indicate are possible?
options: A fine of up to £5,000 only, with no College action once the court has acted
Up to 10 years' prison and/or an unlimited fine, and dismissal where appropriate
Disciplinary action only, as the College's own process replaces any prosecution
Up to 10 years' prison, but no fine and no further disciplinary action by the College
questions.explanation: Individuals convicted of bribery may face up to 10 years in prison and/or an unlimited fine, and the College will also take disciplinary action where appropriate, including dismissal.
questions.source_excerpt: they may face up to 10 years in prison and/or an unlimited fine. ... Take disciplinary action where appropriate, including dismissal or termination of contracts

questions.question: A staff member suspects that the Registrar is involved in a bribery scheme and feels unable to report it to the Registrar. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what should the staff member do?
options: Say nothing, as the duty to report is lifted where the Registrar is involved
Wait for the ARRC's annual review and raise the concern with members then
Raise the concern promptly through the College's Whistleblowing Policy
Note the concern in the register of approved gifts and hospitality items
questions.explanation: Staff must report suspected bribery promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy, so the Whistleblowing route remains open; failing to report may itself be a breach.
questions.source_excerpt: Failure to report concerns may itself be treated as a breach of this policy. ... Staff are required to report any suspected or actual fraud, bribery or corruption promptly to the Registrar or via the Whistleblowing Policy.

questions.question: An investigation substantiates that a self-employed individual working on the College's behalf submitted fraudulent claims. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what action may the College take?
options: Nothing formal, as disciplinary measures apply to employees only
A warning only, as self-employed staff are outside the policy's scope
Asking for repayment only, as legal action is reserved for employees
Contractual or legal action, including termination of the contract
questions.explanation: The policy covers self-employed people working on the College's behalf, and where fraud is substantiated it provides for disciplinary, contractual and/or legal action, including termination of contracts.
questions.source_excerpt: It also extends to anyone working for or on our behalf (e.g., self-employed individuals, agency workers). ... Take disciplinary action where appropriate, including dismissal or termination of contracts ... Where fraud or financial irregularity is substantiated, appropriate disciplinary, contractual and/or legal action will be taken.

questions.question: A new starter joins the College in a role it has classed as higher-risk for fraud and bribery. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which training should they expect?
options: Mandatory induction, periodic refreshers and enhanced training
Enhanced higher-risk training, which replaces the standard induction
Mandatory induction only, as refreshers are for longer-serving staff
Enhanced training only once an incident has occurred in their team
questions.explanation: All staff receive mandatory induction and periodic refresher training, and those in higher-risk roles also receive enhanced training.
questions.source_excerpt: This includes mandatory induction training, periodic refresher training and enhanced training for higher-risk roles.

questions.question: While scoring tenders, a staff member is offered an interest-free personal loan by one of the bidders, which hopes for a favourable score. How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy's definition of bribery apply to this loan?
options: It falls outside it, as a loan must be repaid and gives no lasting advantage
It falls within it, as the definition covers any gift, loan, payment or advantage
It falls within it only if the loan is later written off rather than repaid
It falls outside it, as the definition is limited to cash and physical gifts
questions.explanation: The policy defines bribery as offering or accepting any gift, loan, payment, reward or advantage as an encouragement to do something dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust, so a loan is expressly covered.
questions.source_excerpt: the offering or accepting of any gift, loan, payment, reward or advantage for personal gain as an encouragement to do something which is dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust.

questions.question: An applicant's parent offers a lecturer an expensive watch 'to help with the marks'. A colleague suggests asking the Principal to authorise it as a gift. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which route is correct?
options: Ask the Principal to authorise it in advance, then have it registered
Accept it, then declare it to the Registrar for the gifts register
Refuse it and report it immediately to the Registrar as a bribe
Refuse it and ask the Principal to note the offer on the register
questions.explanation: Gifts may be authorised only where nothing is expected in return; an offer made to influence marks is a bribe, which must be refused and reported immediately to the Registrar.
questions.source_excerpt: If a bribe is offered or solicited, it must be refused unless personal safety is at risk and reported immediately to the Registrar. ... reasonable and proportionate gifts and hospitality may support positive relationships where nothing is expected in return.

questions.question: To avoid paying anything themselves, a College staff member asks a self-employed agent acting for the College to offer a school counsellor cash to steer pupils towards the College. Who breaches the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy?
options: Both: the staff member indirectly, and the agent as someone acting for the College
Only the agent, as the staff member made no payment and offered nothing directly
Only the staff member, as self-employed agents fall outside the policy's scope
Neither, as the counsellor is not a public official and no student was harmed
questions.explanation: The policy prohibits bribery by any employee or person acting for or on behalf of the College, whether directly or indirectly, so both the staff member and the agent are in breach.
questions.source_excerpt: At LCC it is strictly prohibited for any employee or person acting for or on behalf of the College to engage in bribery, fraud or corrupt practices, directly or indirectly.

questions.question: An admissions manager says the College's fraud risk assessments and internal controls concern finance only and do not reach admissions. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, which statement is correct?
options: Admissions is assessed only after a fraud has been reported within it
Risks are assessed across operations including finance and admissions
Only finance and procurement are assessed; admissions sets its own rules
Admissions is covered by the ARRC's annual report rather than by controls
questions.explanation: The College assesses fraud risks across its operations, expressly including finance, procurement, admissions and partnerships, and applies proportionate internal controls to the risks identified.
questions.source_excerpt: The College assesses fraud risks at least annually, and in response to material changes, across its operations, including finance, procurement, admissions and partnerships. Proportionate internal controls, including segregation of duties, approval processes, reconciliations and due diligence are implemented to mitigate identified risks

questions.question: A College officer offers a foreign visa officer free places on College short courses for his children, in return for faster student visas. How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy treat this?
options: It is not bribery, as no money or physical gift changes hands at all
It is bribery only if the visas are in fact issued faster as a result
It is permitted if the Principal authorises the places in advance as a gift
It is bribing a foreign public official, as anything of value can count
questions.explanation: Bribery can involve anything of value, not just money, and bribing a foreign public official is a criminal offence under the Bribery Act 2010; offering the advantage is enough.
questions.source_excerpt: c) bribe a foreign public official; ... It is a form of corruption involving money, gifts, hospitality, or anything of value as an inducement or reward for dishonest or illegal conduct.

questions.question: An applicant's relative offers a staff member a paid weekend away to let the applicant sit an internal test late without the usual approval. The staff member argues that bending an internal rule is not illegal. How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy's definition of bribery apply?
options: It is outside the definition, as the favour asked for must be a criminal act
It is within the definition, which covers dishonesty and breaches of trust
It is outside the definition, as a weekend away is hospitality, not a reward
It is within the definition only if the relative is a public official
questions.explanation: The policy's definition covers an advantage offered as an encouragement to do something dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust, so the favour need not be illegal.
questions.source_excerpt: the offering or accepting of any gift, loan, payment, reward or advantage for personal gain as an encouragement to do something which is dishonest, illegal or a breach of trust.

questions.question: A College manager offers a UK council inspector £500 to overlook a missing fire-safety certificate, arguing that the Bribery Act 2010 offence involving officials covers only foreign public officials. According to the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, is the manager right?
options: No, offering a bribe is itself an offence, whoever the recipient is
Yes, UK officials are covered by public-sector rules outside this policy
Yes, provided the payment is declared to the Registrar for the register
Yes, as no offence arises unless the inspector accepts the money
questions.explanation: The policy lists offering, promising or giving a bribe as an offence with no limit on who receives it; bribing a foreign public official is a separate, additional offence.
questions.source_excerpt: Under the Bribery Act 2010, it is a criminal offence to: a) offer, promise or give a bribe; b) request, agree to receive or accept a bribe; c) bribe a foreign public official

questions.question: A senior manager tells a junior finance officer to process a 'consultancy' payment to a third party that the officer suspects is for improper benefit, insisting that only the manager is accountable as the more senior person. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what should the officer do?
options: Process it, as accountability rests with the senior manager who gave the order
Decline to process it, but say nothing so as not to accuse a senior colleague
Process it, and raise a concern only if a later audit finds it was improper
Report the suspicion promptly, as the policy applies regardless of seniority
questions.explanation: The policy applies to all employees regardless of role or seniority, bans payments to third parties for improper benefit and requires suspected bribery to be reported promptly, so a senior instruction does not remove the duty.
questions.source_excerpt: This policy applies to all employees of London Churchill College, regardless of role or seniority. ... c) Making payments to third parties for improper benefit ... Suspected bribery must also be reported promptly, even if the individual is not directly involved.

questions.question: A catering firm bidding for a College contract offers to pay for the wedding reception of the procurement officer's daughter, hoping for a favourable decision. The officer says nothing is being given to them personally. How does the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy treat the offer?
options: It is allowed, as the officer's daughter falls outside the policy's scope
It is prohibited, as bribery is banned in any form, directly or indirectly
It is a gift to a relative, so it needs the Principal's authorisation first
It is allowed if the daughter declares it to the Registrar for the register
questions.explanation: Bribery is prohibited directly or indirectly and in any form, so routing the advantage to a relative does not make it acceptable; gifts are acceptable only where nothing is expected in return.
questions.source_excerpt: strictly prohibited for any employee or person acting for or on behalf of the College to engage in bribery, fraud or corrupt practices, directly or indirectly. This includes: a) Offering, giving, requesting, or accepting bribes in any form to gain advantage ... where nothing is expected in return

questions.question: An agency worker in the College's procurement team is invited by an existing supplier to a hosted business lunch to review the contract. The worker's agency says its staff follow only the agency's own gifts code. Under the Anti-Bribery and Anti-Corruption Policy, what is the correct position?
options: The agency's code applies instead, so no College approval is needed at all
The policy applies, but hosted hospitality needs recording, not approval
The policy applies, and the Registrar may approve the lunch afterwards
The policy applies, and the Principal must authorise the lunch in advance
questions.explanation: The policy extends to agency workers acting for the College, and all gifts and hospitality, hosted or not, must be authorised in advance by the Principal; the Registrar only keeps the register.
questions.source_excerpt: It also extends to anyone working for or on our behalf (e.g., self-employed individuals, agency workers). ... b) All gifts and hospitality must be authorised in advance by the Principal c) The Registrar maintains a register of approved items

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, once a Collaborative Procedures Manual (CPM) has been approved by both partners, how does it relate to the responsibilities listed in the policy?
options: The policy's listed responsibilities take priority wherever the two conflict
The CPM binds the partner, while the listed responsibilities continue to bind the College
The CPM takes effect once the first full year of programme delivery has been completed
The approved CPM prevails over the responsibilities listed in the policy
questions.explanation: The policy states that once both partners have approved the CPM, it prevails over the responsibilities listed in the policy's tables.
questions.source_excerpt: Once the CPM has been approved by both partners it shall prevail over the responsibilities listed below.

questions.question: Shortly before a new academic year, the awarding body of a franchised programme has not told the College of any programme changes. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what should happen?
options: Assume nothing has changed, since it is the awarding body's responsibility to notify the College of changes
The Senior Quality Assurance Officer contacts the awarding body's representative to confirm any changes
Wait for the External Examiner to report any programme changes at the next scheduled Examination Board
Deliver last year's version of the programme and update it once the awarding body issues a formal notice
questions.explanation: Although the awarding body should notify changes, the College must follow up: the Senior Quality Assurance Officer contacts the awarding body's designated representative before each academic year.
questions.source_excerpt: the College is responsible for following up to ensure that this is the case. Consequently, the College's Senior Quality Assurance Officer will contact the designated representative of the awarding body prior to the beginning of each academic year to confirm what changes to the programme, if any, have been made.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is the College's primary responsibility when it acts as a designated (Study) Centre?
options: Teaching the programme and first marking assessments on behalf of the awarding body
Registering students and making the final decisions on who enters the programme
Providing the agreed space and resources to deliver programmes owned by the awarding body
Designing, developing and managing its own programmes for validation by the partner
questions.explanation: As a Study Centre, the College's primary role is to provide the agreed space and resources; the awarding body registers students and carries out teaching.
questions.source_excerpt: As a Study Centre, the College's primary responsibility is to provide the space and resources agreed to deliver programmes owned by an awarding body. The awarding body is responsible for registering students and carrying out teaching.

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which responsibilities can the College be expected to take on for franchised provision?
options: Teaching, first marking of assessments, providing feedback and a greater monitoring role
Appointing the External Examiner and confirming final award decisions for the programme
Providing the agreed space and resources, with the awarding body registering students and teaching
Designing its own programmes and setting entry requirements independently of the awarding body
questions.explanation: The policy states that franchised provision is delivered by the College, with responsibilities expected to include teaching, first marking, providing feedback and a greater role in monitoring the programme.
questions.source_excerpt: Franchised provision is delivered by the College and its responsibilities can be expected to include teaching, first marking of assessments, providing feedback and a greater role in monitoring the programme.

questions.question: An applicant to a franchised programme has been provisionally offered a place by the College after meeting the entry requirements. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who makes the final decision about the student?
options: The awarding body, which may base it on detailed evidence provided by the College
The Registrar, whose provisional offer becomes final once the entry requirements have been met
The College's Academic Board, after reviewing the applicant's entry testing results and references
The Head of Programme, acting on the recommendation of the College's admissions team
questions.explanation: The College makes provisional offers, but the policy states that the awarding body makes the final decisions about students registered on its programmes, possibly using the College's detailed evidence.
questions.source_excerpt: The Awarding Body will exercise responsibility for making the final decisions about students registered on its programmes, but decisions may be based upon the detailed evidence provided by the College.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, how does the College determine and manage risk in relation to its collaborative partnerships?
options: By relying on the awarding body's own risk assessment, since the programmes and awards belong to the partner
By commissioning an external audit once the partnership has completed its first full year of programme delivery
By reviewing the partnership once a student complaint or academic appeal relating to it has been formally upheld
By due diligence before approval and ongoing use of the institutional Risk Register and student protection plan
questions.explanation: The policy states that risk is determined and managed through due diligence before approval and on an ongoing basis through the institutional Risk Register and student protection plan.
questions.source_excerpt: Determine and manage risk by conducting due diligence in respect of partnerships prior to approval, and on an ongoing basis through the institutional Risk Register and student protection plan;

questions.question: A student on a franchised programme comes to you with a concern about their course. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who is responsible for discussing and resolving the concern in the first instance?
options: The awarding body, as the owner of the franchised programme
The External Examiner assigned to the programme by the awarding body
The Office for Students, as the regulator of collaborative provision
The College, as the provider delivering the franchised programme
questions.explanation: For franchised programmes, the policy makes the College responsible for discussing and resolving issues and concerns raised by students in the first instance.
questions.source_excerpt: The College is responsible for discussing and resolving issues and concerns voiced by students in the first instance

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what information must the College provide to students on collaborative programmes about complaints?
options: Details of the College's own complaints procedure, as awarding bodies inform their students separately
Accessible, trustworthy information on the complaints procedures open to them, including the awarding body's
Information about the complaints procedures once a student has formally requested it from the College in writing
Contact details for the Office for Students as the first point of complaint for partnership programme students
questions.explanation: The policy commits the College to give students accessible and trustworthy information about all complaints procedures they can use, including those of awarding bodies.
questions.source_excerpt: Provide students with accessible and trustworthy information about the complaints procedures to which they have access, including those of awarding bodies;

questions.question: You are on a team designing a new programme that the College intends to submit to a partner for validation. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what must happen before it is submitted for the partner's approval?
options: The programme must first run for a full year under a Study Centre arrangement
The awarding body's External Examiner must sign off the programme's assessment briefs
Students must be provisionally recruited to demonstrate sufficient demand for it
An internal approval event must take place at the College, with Academic Board sign-off
questions.explanation: For validated programmes, the policy requires an internal approval event at the College and Academic Board, with sign-off sought before submission to the partner.
questions.source_excerpt: An internal approval event will take place at the College and Academic Board. Sign-off will be sought prior to submitting the programme for the partner's approval.

questions.question: A College lecturer has drafted a new assessment for a franchised programme. According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is likely to be required before the assessment is used at the College?
options: Review and approval by the University (the awarding body) before being used
Approval by the module's elected student representatives before release
Sign-off by the Office for Students as the sector regulator for partnerships
Sign-off by the College's Registrar before its release to students
questions.explanation: The policy notes that local staff may help design franchised assessments, but these are likely to need the University's review and approval before being used at the College.
questions.source_excerpt: Local teaching staff may also play a role in assessment design, although it is likely that the assessments would require the review and approval of the University before being used at the College.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who is responsible for appointing the External Examiner assigned to a partnership programme?
options: The College's Academic Board
The awarding body for the programme
The Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring
The Senior Quality Assurance Officer
questions.explanation: The policy states that the appointment of the External Examiner is the responsibility of the awarding body.
questions.source_excerpt: The appointment of the External Examiner is the responsibility of the awarding body.

questions.question: For a validated programme, the partner has delegated responsibility for making offers to prospective students to the College. According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what should the College do?
options: Apply its own entry criteria independently, as the partner no longer has any role in admissions decisions
Refer applications to the External Examiner to confirm that the agreed entry criteria have been met
Work with the partner on extra measures so entry criteria are applied consistently, e.g. partner screening
Set its own entry requirements, since those agreed at the validation event lapse once offer-making is delegated
questions.explanation: Where offer-making is delegated, the policy says the College will work with the partner to put additional measures in place, such as screening of applications by partner staff, so entry criteria are applied consistently.
questions.source_excerpt: The responsibility for making offers to prospective students may be delegated to the College. In such a case, the College will work with the partner to put in place any additional measures to allow the partner to ensure entry criteria are applied consistently. This might include screening of applications by a member of staff at the partner.

questions.question: The awarding body is completing the annual monitoring report for a franchised programme delivered at the College. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what else must the College do?
options: Nothing further, as the awarding body's report replaces any internal College monitoring report
Complete its own report if the awarding body specifically requests one, otherwise nothing further
Supply requested documentation and also complete its own internal annual monitoring report
Submit its own monitoring report directly to the Office for Students instead of to the partner
questions.explanation: For franchised programmes, the College provides any documentation the awarding body requests and, in addition, completes its own internal annual monitoring report.
questions.source_excerpt: for which the College will provide any documentation requested by them. In addition to the awarding body's report, the College will complete its own internal annual monitoring report that includes a critical reflection on progress made in each year

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the guiding principles for assessment in the Collaborative Partnerships Policy?
options: Reasonable adjustments are made available to students with disabilities and additional needs
Award decisions are confirmed by the Examination Board in line with awarding body regulations
Students are assessed repeatedly on each learning outcome to maximise evidence of achievement
Assessment tasks are based on published assessment criteria or the learning outcomes of the units
questions.explanation: The assessment principles state that students will not be over-assessed on learning outcomes, so repeated assessment of each outcome is not a principle; the other three options are listed principles.
questions.source_excerpt: assessment tasks are based on published assessment criteria or learning outcomes of the units ... Reasonable adjustments are made available to students with disabilities and additional needs ... Students will not be over-assessed on learning outcomes ... Ensure the awards decisions are confirmed by the Examination Board in accordance with awarding body regulations.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which programmes are considered by the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR)?
options: All programmes, regardless of the type of provision they fall under
Validated programmes, since the College owns their design
Franchised and validated programmes, but not Study Centre provision
Programmes with unresolved anomalies that have been reported to the awarding body
questions.explanation: The annual monitoring principles state that all programmes, regardless of provision type, are considered by the CAMR.
questions.source_excerpt: All programmes, regardless of the provision type, are considered by the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR).

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which body takes full responsibility for the robust implementation and management of the College's internal processes relating to collaborative provision?
options: The Academic Board, acting on advice from each awarding body
The Principal's Executive Group (PEG), in consultation with key College boards
The Quality Department, reporting to the College Oversight Board
The Board of Directors, advised by the College's Senior Quality Assurance Officer
questions.explanation: The policy places full responsibility for implementing and managing internal collaborative-provision processes on the PEG, in consultation with the BoD, the COB and the Academic Board.
questions.source_excerpt: The Principal's Executive Group (PEG), in consultation with the Board of Directors (BoD), the College Oversight Board (COB) and the Academic Board, takes full responsibility for the robust implementation and management of internal processes relating to collaborative provision.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what must the College ensure before a collaborative venture agreed with an awarding body commences?
options: That sufficient time is taken to plan academic and operational matters, such as programme fit
That the first student cohort has been recruited and provisionally admitted by the Registrar
That the programme has first run for a full year under a Study Centre arrangement
That an External Examiner has been appointed by the College's own Academic Board
questions.explanation: The policy requires sufficient time to plan academic and operational matters before collaborative ventures begin, with programme fit, resources, recruitment, teaching and assessment and student support particularly important.
questions.source_excerpt: Ensure that sufficient time is taken to plan academic and operational matters prior to the commencement of collaborative ventures agreed with awarding bodies. In this context, programme fit, resource allocation, recruitment, learning, teaching and assessment practices and student support are particularly important;

questions.question: The Collaborative Partnerships Policy requires the College to discuss how each partnership relationship will be managed, and possible decisions if the partnership is terminated. At what level must this discussion take place?
options: At programme committee meetings with student representatives
At departmental level, led by the Head of Programme
At a senior committee level within the College
At the annual External Examiner review meeting
questions.explanation: The policy states that how the relationship will be managed, and possible decisions on termination, are discussed at a senior committee level.
questions.source_excerpt: Discuss at a senior committee level how the relationship will be managed and make possible decisions in the event of the termination of the partnership;

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which new programmes must receive Academic Board approval?
options: Validated programmes only, as the College owns their design
Only those to be delivered in person on the College's campuses
Only franchised programmes where College staff set assessments
All new programmes, regardless of mode or method of delivery
questions.explanation: The policy commits the College to secure Academic Board approval for all new programmes, whatever their mode or method of delivery.
questions.source_excerpt: Secure Academic Board approval for all new programmes, regardless of mode or method of delivery;

questions.question: The Collaborative Partnerships Policy describes Study Centre, franchised and validated provision. How does the policy say these descriptions of types of provision should be treated?
options: As fixed categories that every partnership agreement must follow
As a guide only, since each partnership is unique
As binding definitions that override an approved CPM
As the only three arrangements the College may enter into
questions.explanation: The policy presents the types of provision as examples and states that, because each partnership is unique, the descriptions are intended as a guide only.
questions.source_excerpt: The following are examples of types of provision that could be offered through a collaborative partnership. Please note that each partnership is unique, and these descriptions are intended as a guide only.

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, why might a Study Centre arrangement be used before a partnership progresses to franchised or validated provision?
options: To let the College design its own programmes before seeking their validation
To meet an Office for Students rule that every new partnership starts this way
To let College staff build a record of first marking before a franchise begins
To test the partnership's suitability, as it carries less risk for the awarding body
questions.explanation: The policy notes that Study Centre provision involves less risk for the awarding body and might be used to determine the suitability of the partnership before franchised or validated provision.
questions.source_excerpt: This type of provision involves less risk for the awarding body, as fewer responsibilities are devolved to the partner, and might be used to determine the suitability of the partnership prior to progressing to either Franchised or Validated provision.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what does validated provision give the College the opportunity to do?
options: Design, develop and manage its own programmes, taking more ownership of them
Deliver the awarding body's own programmes, with teaching and first marking
Provide agreed space and resources while the awarding body does the teaching
Appoint its own External Examiners and confirm final awards independently
questions.explanation: The policy states that validated programmes let the College design, develop and manage its own programmes and procedures, giving it more ownership of the programme offered.
questions.source_excerpt: Validated programmes provide the College with opportunities for designing, developing and managing their own programmes and operational procedures, which allows the College to adopt more ownership over the programme offered.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, when do the College's guiding principles listed at the top of each table in the policy's appendix apply?
options: For validated programmes, where the College owns the programme design
Until both partners have approved the Collaborative Procedures Manual
At all times, whatever type of provision is being offered by the College
Where the awarding body has no equivalent principle set out in its own policies
questions.explanation: The policy states that, regardless of the type of provision being offered, the guiding principles always apply, which is why they head each table.
questions.source_excerpt: Regardless of the type of provision being offered, these principles shall always apply and are therefore listed at the top of each table (see appendix).

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, once changes to a franchised programme have been confirmed with the awarding body, where must those changes be entered?
options: In the institutional Risk Register used to manage partnership risk
In the Quality Department's register of collaborative programmes
In the Registrar's student records for the affected cohort
In the minutes of the next partnership meeting with the awarding body
questions.explanation: The policy requires records of relevant communication to be kept and the changes to be entered in the Quality Department's register of collaborative programmes.
questions.source_excerpt: Records of relevant communication must be retained, and the changes entered in the Quality Department's register of collaborative programmes.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, why should changes to a franchised programme be uploaded to the College's website at the earliest available opportunity?
options: Because the changes may influence a potential candidate's choice
Because the awarding body reviews the website before each academic year
Because the Office for Students must see changes before they take effect
Because enrolled students must accept the changes online before teaching
questions.explanation: The policy asks for programme changes to be uploaded to the website at the earliest opportunity because they may influence a potential candidate's choice.
questions.source_excerpt: Uploading any changes to the programme onto the College's website at the earliest available opportunity, as changes may ... influence a potential candidate's choice.

questions.question: According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who oversees the recruitment, selection and provisional admission of applicants to franchised programmes?
options: The Quality Department
The awarding body's Link Tutor
The College's Registrar
The Head of Programme
questions.explanation: For franchised programmes, the policy states that the Registrar will oversee the process of recruiting, selecting and provisionally admitting applicants.
questions.source_excerpt: Recruiting, selecting and provisionally admitting applicants wishing to register on a particular franchised programme. The Registrar will oversee the process.

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, how is student feedback on a franchised programme dealt with when it falls under the awarding body's responsibilities?
options: It is sent to the External Examiner for comment at the Exam Board
It is held back until the College's annual monitoring report is written
It is returned to students to raise with the awarding body themselves
It is discussed with the awarding body through partnership meetings
questions.explanation: The policy states that feedback falling under the awarding body's responsibilities is discussed through partnership meetings.
questions.source_excerpt: Feedback that falls under the responsibilities of the awarding body are discussed through partnership meetings.

questions.question: According to the assessment guiding principles in the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, under which policy should academic malpractice be dealt with where necessary?
options: The Academic Discipline Policy
The Internal Verification Policy
The Student Conduct and Disciplinary Policy
The Programme Modification Policy
questions.explanation: The assessment guiding principles state that, where necessary, academic malpractice should be dealt with under the Academic Discipline Policy.
questions.source_excerpt: Good academic practice must be maintained and where necessary academic malpractice should be dealt with under the Academic Discipline Policy.

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, to whom does the College submit assessment results and marked samples for review and comment before the Examination Board?
options: The Office for Students and the College's Academic Board
The awarding body's Link Tutor and the programme's External Examiner
The Registrar and the programme's elected student representatives
The Quality Department and the Principal's Executive Group (PEG)
questions.explanation: The policy requires assessment results and marked samples to go to the awarding body's Link Tutor and the programme's External Examiner in good time before the Examination Board.
questions.source_excerpt: Submitting assessment results and marked samples to the Link Tutor (title may vary) of the awarding body and to the External Examiner assigned to the programme in good time for adequate review and comment prior to the Examination Board.

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, for Study Centre and franchised provision, how must the College notify the awarding body of unresolved anomalies or problems arising in the provision?
options: It must hold them over for inclusion in the annual monitoring report
It may raise them informally through the student representatives
It must report them to the partner explicitly and in a timely manner
It must wait until the External Examiner has confirmed them
questions.explanation: For Study Centre and franchised provision, the policy requires the College to notify the awarding body of unresolved anomalies or problems explicitly and in a timely manner.
questions.source_excerpt: Notifying the awarding body of unresolved anomalies or problems arising in the provision explicitly and in a timely manner

questions.question: A new collaborative partnership is being set up and its Collaborative Procedures Manual (CPM) is being drafted. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who develops the CPM and how are the appendix tables in the policy used?
options: The awarding body drafts it alone, and the tables are later used to audit the College's compliance
The College develops it with the partner, using the tables as guidance and as a checklist of coverage
The Quality Department drafts it after the first year, using the tables as a template for its reports
The College drafts it alone, and the tables override the CPM wherever the two set out different duties
questions.explanation: The policy requires a CPM for any new partnership, developed together with the partner, and says the appendix tables give guidance during its development and act as a checklist that it covers the necessary ground.
questions.source_excerpt: Ensure the production of a Collaborative Procedures Manual (CPM) for any new partnership, working together with the partner to develop it ... The tables in the appendix will provide guidance during the development of a CPM and will act as a checklist to ensure that the CPM covers the necessary ground for the partnership to function effectively.

questions.question: Before the first delivery of a franchised programme, a lecturer notices that the College's module handbook shows older module codes than the awarding body's latest documentation. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what must the College ensure?
options: Delivery follows the version in the original partnership agreement until the next periodic review
Delivery follows the College's own module handbook, as the College carries out the franchised teaching
Delivery reflects the awarding body's most recent changes, notably to module codes and assessments
Delivery continues unchanged and the difference is noted for the College's next annual monitoring report
questions.explanation: The College must deliver franchised programmes in line with the approved documentation and reflect the awarding body's most recent changes, particularly module identification codes and assessments, so it offers the most current version.
questions.source_excerpt: Ensuring that the delivery of franchised programmes are in line with the approved programme documentation and that it reflects the most recent changes made by the awarding body, particularly in respect of module identification codes and assessments.

questions.question: The College is planning a Study Centre arrangement and expects that, after the first year, its own academic staff will teach students registered on the programme. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, how should this planned change be handled?
options: It should be included in the plan brought to the Academic Board's attention
It should be agreed informally with the awarding body once the first year ends
It should be raised with the External Examiner at the first Examination Board
It should be logged in the Risk Register and reviewed once the first year ends
questions.explanation: For Study Centre provision, changes planned for after the first year, such as College academic staff teaching registered students, should be included in the plan brought to the Academic Board's attention.
questions.source_excerpt: If changes in requirements are planned to take place after the first year of provision: for example, academic staff members are allowed to teach students registered on the programme, then this should be included as part of the plan brought to the Academic Board's attention.

questions.question: A programme team is designing a new programme that the College will put forward for validation by an awarding body. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, how is this normally done and against which criteria is the programme assessed?
options: Through a validation request drafted by the partner, assessed against the awarding body's benchmarks alone
Through a Study Centre resource plan, assessed against the criteria in the Collaborative Procedures Manual
Through an External Examiner proposal, assessed against the Office for Students' registration conditions
Through a Programme Approval Form, assessed against the College's Programme Design Policy and the partner's
questions.explanation: For validated provision the College designs new programmes, normally by completing a Programme Approval Form, and the programme is assessed against the College's Programme Design Policy criteria and the partner's equivalent policy.
questions.source_excerpt: The College will take responsibility for designing new programmes for the validation of the awarding body. This would normally be through the completion of a Programme Approval Form. The Programme will be assessed against the criteria set by the College's Programme Design Policy (and the respective policy of the partner).

questions.question: An applicant to a franchised programme meets the awarding body's entry requirements but not the College's own requirements. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, on what basis can a place be offered provisionally?
options: Meeting the awarding body's requirements alone, as the College's own requirements are advisory
Meeting both the awarding body's requirements and the requirements of the College
Meeting either set of requirements, provided the Registrar records the reason for the offer
Meeting the College's requirements alone, as the awarding body makes the final decision later
questions.explanation: Places on franchised programmes are offered provisionally only where candidates meet both the awarding body's requirements and the College's requirements, so this applicant cannot yet be offered a place.
questions.source_excerpt: The Registrar will oversee the process. Places will be offered provisionally on the basis of candidates meeting the awarding body's requirements and the requirements of the College.

questions.question: Some students on a programme the College hosts as a Study Centre are unfamiliar with the College and its ethos. According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, why can this happen?
options: The College must accept any applicant referred to it by the Office for Students
The College fills Study Centre places only through its own clearing process
The awarding body may recruit from a number of sources, not only the College
The Registrar delegates all Study Centre offers to external recruitment agents
questions.explanation: In a Study Centre arrangement the College may recommend its own applicants, but the awarding body may recruit from a number of sources, so students unfamiliar with the College may join the programme.
questions.source_excerpt: Although the College may recommend applicants from its own programmes, the awarding body may recruit from a number of sources. Consequently, students unfamiliar with the College and its ethos may be recruited to the programme.

questions.question: Student feedback on a franchised programme has been gathered through End of Term Student Surveys and analysed in Student Feedback Reports. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who determines the responses to that feedback?
options: The Principal's Executive Group (PEG)
The programme's elected student representatives
The awarding body's Link Tutor for the programme
The External Examiner for the programme
questions.explanation: For franchised programmes, feedback is analysed through Student Feedback Reports and the responses to it are determined by the PEG.
questions.source_excerpt: through End of Term Student Surveys (completed for each module) and comments made by student representatives. Feedback is analysed through Student Feedback Reports and responses to the feedback is determined by the PEG.

questions.question: A student on a programme the College hosts as a Study Centre raises a query about library and IT facilities. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is the College's student engagement role for this type of provision?
options: Referring every student query to the awarding body, which alone responds on engagement matters
Appointing the student representatives itself and deciding the responses to all student feedback
Collecting formal written complaints only, which it forwards to the External Examiner for review
Responding to queries on resources and facilities, and supporting the selection of student reps
questions.explanation: For Study Centre provision, the College supports the awarding body in selecting student representatives and responds to queries from students about resources and facilities.
questions.source_excerpt: Supporting the awarding body in selecting student representatives and responding to queries from the student body in relation to resources and facilities.

questions.question: For a validated programme, the College has set up structures for designing and approving assessment briefs and for marking and moderating summative work. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who oversees and who monitors these structures?
options: Overviewed by the Senior Quality Assurance Officer and monitored by the External Examiner
Overviewed by the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring; monitored by the Senior QA Officer
Overviewed by the Registrar and monitored by the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring
Overviewed by the awarding body's Link Tutor and monitored by the College's Quality Department
questions.explanation: For validated programmes, the assessment design, approval, marking and moderation structures are overviewed by the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring and monitored by the Senior Quality Assurance Officer.
questions.source_excerpt: Establishing robust structures for the design and approval of assessment briefs and the marking and moderation of summative assessments, which will be overviewed by the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring and monitored by the Senior Quality Assurance Officer.

questions.question: Assessment results for a franchised programme delivered by the College are ready for confirmation. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, whose regulations normally govern the assessment and which Exam Board considers the results?
options: The College's regulations, with results considered by the College's own Exam Board
The Office for Students' rules, with results considered by the College's Academic Board
The awarding body's regulations, with results considered by the awarding body's Exam Board
The College's regulations, with results considered by a joint board chaired by the Registrar
questions.explanation: Under a franchise arrangement, assessment normally follows the awarding body's regulations and the results are considered by the awarding body's Exam Board.
questions.source_excerpt: Assessment under a franchise arrangement would normally be conducted in line with the awarding body's regulations and results would be considered by the Exam Board of the awarding body.

questions.question: For a validated programme, a colleague asks what annual monitoring report the College itself is expected to produce. According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is the correct answer?
options: A joint report written with the Link Tutor once the External Examiner's report is received
A short summary of student survey results, sent to the External Examiner before the Exam Board
A report only where anomalies remain unresolved, sent to the awarding body in a timely manner
A full annual monitoring report, typically on College templates, including critical reflection
questions.explanation: For validated programmes, the College completes a full annual monitoring report, typically using its internal templates, with critical reflection, Good Practice and recommendations for improvement.
questions.source_excerpt: Complete a full annual monitoring report, typically using the College's internal templates. The report will include a critical reflection on progress made in each year, identifies Good Practice and makes recommendations for improvement.

questions.question: A programme leader is drafting an individual programme report as part of annual monitoring. According to the guiding principles in the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what should the report include?
options: Key actions to be taken in the following year, together with student satisfaction indicators
A ranking of teaching staff by module pass rates, plus the individual grades awarded to each student
Only the items requiring improvement, with good practice reported separately to the PEG
A summary of the awarding body's report, without separate College reflection or actions
questions.explanation: The annual monitoring principles say individual programme reports should identify key actions for the following year and include student satisfaction indicators.
questions.source_excerpt: Individual programme reports should identify key actions to be taken during the following year and should include student satisfaction indicators

questions.question: The College is moving from franchised to validated provision with a partner. According to the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what does the College recognise that the added freedom to develop its own programmes brings?
options: Added responsibility for robust internal systems that meet UK regulators' and the partner's needs
Fewer reporting duties, since the awarding body no longer monitors programme quality or standards
Freedom to set its own entry requirements for the programme without needing to agree them with the partner
Exemption from Academic Board approval, since the partner validates and approves the programme instead
questions.explanation: The policy recognises that the freedom of validated provision brings added responsibilities for robust internal structures and systems that meet UK regulatory and quality bodies' and the awarding body's requirements.
questions.source_excerpt: The College recognises that the freedom gained in developing its own programmes will engender added responsibilities for ensuring that internal structures and systems for managing the provision are robust and meet the requirements and expectations of the United Kingdom Regulatory and Quality bodies, as well as those determined by the awarding body.

questions.question: A partner proposes an arrangement it calls a franchise: it would own the programme, register the students and carry out the teaching, while the College provides the agreed space and resources. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which type of provision does this match?
options: Franchised provision, as the programme is owned and approved by the awarding body
A designated Study Centre, as the College's role in delivery would be limited
Validated provision, as the partner would validate the programme and register students
Franchised provision, as the teaching would take place on the College's own site
questions.explanation: Where the awarding body owns the programme, registers students and teaches while the College provides agreed space and resources, the policy describes a Study Centre, in which the College's involvement in delivery is limited.
questions.source_excerpt: As a Study Centre, the College's primary responsibility is to provide the space and resources agreed to deliver programmes owned by an awarding body. The awarding body is responsible for registering students and carrying out teaching. ... The College's involvement in the actual delivery and operational processes is limited.

questions.question: Both partners have approved a Collaborative Procedures Manual (CPM) that allocates some duties differently from the appendix tables in the Collaborative Partnerships Policy. What is the status of the guiding principles listed at the top of each table?
options: They still apply, while the CPM prevails over the specific responsibilities
They are set aside along with the listed duties, as the CPM prevails over both
They apply only to matters that the approved CPM does not itself cover in detail
They are replaced by the awarding body's own principles once the CPM is approved
questions.explanation: An approved CPM prevails over the responsibilities listed in the tables, but the policy states that the guiding principles shall always apply regardless of the type of provision.
questions.source_excerpt: Once the CPM has been approved by both partners it shall prevail over the responsibilities listed below. ... Regardless of the type of provision being offered, these principles shall always apply and are therefore listed at the top of each table (see appendix).

questions.question: A draft Collaborative Procedures Manual (CPM) for a new partnership has been approved by the College but not yet by the partner. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, does it yet prevail over the responsibilities listed in the policy?
options: Yes, because the College led its drafting and the College's own approval is sufficient
Yes, provided the Quality Department has checked it against the appendix checklist
No, it prevails only after it has been used for one full academic year of delivery
No, it prevails over the listed responsibilities only once both partners approve it
questions.explanation: The CPM is developed with the partner and prevails over the listed responsibilities only once it has been approved by both partners, so College approval alone is not enough.
questions.source_excerpt: Ensure the production of a Collaborative Procedures Manual (CPM) for any new partnership, working together with the partner to develop it ... Once the CPM has been approved by both partners it shall prevail over the responsibilities listed below.

questions.question: An applicant to a franchised programme meets both the awarding body's and the College's entry requirements, but the College's admission tests point to weak prospects of completing. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what must the provisional judgement do?
options: Take prospects for successful completion into account, with tests showing the basis for it
Offer a place automatically, since meeting both sets of entry requirements is sufficient
Refer the applicant to the awarding body, which alone may weigh prospects of completion
Set the test results aside, since admission tests only confirm English language ability
questions.explanation: Meeting both sets of requirements is the basis for a provisional offer, but provisional judgements must also take prospects for successful completion into account, with testing methods showing the basis of the decision.
questions.source_excerpt: Places will be offered provisionally on the basis of candidates meeting the awarding body's requirements and the requirements of the College. Provisional judgements regarding student admissions must take prospects for successful completion into account, and testing methods should demonstrate the basis on which preliminary decisions have been made.

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which statement correctly contrasts how decisions on programme entrants are made for Study Centre provision and for validated provision?
options: Study Centre: the College makes final decisions; validated: the partner must always make offers
Study Centre: the awarding body decides entrants; validated: offers may be delegated to the College
Study Centre: the Registrar decides provisionally; validated: the External Examiner confirms offers
In both: the College makes final decisions and notifies the awarding body after enrolment
questions.explanation: For a Study Centre the awarding body makes the final decision on programme entrants, whereas for validated provision the responsibility for making offers may be delegated to the College.
questions.source_excerpt: The awarding body will make the final decision on programme entrants. ... The responsibility for making offers to prospective students may be delegated to the College.

questions.question: The College hosts an awarding body's programme as a Study Centre. An examination will take place on College premises and a disabled student needs adjustments. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is the College's role?
options: Setting and first marking the exam under College regulations, as it is held on site
Deciding the adjustments under its own policy, then informing the awarding body
None, since the awarding body alone handles every assessment matter at a Study Centre
Supporting the adjustments and ensuring the exam follows the awarding body's regulations
questions.explanation: For Study Centre provision, the College supports the implementation of reasonable adjustments and ensures any on-site examinations are conducted in line with the awarding body's regulations.
questions.source_excerpt: Responsible for supporting the implementation of any reasonable adjustments for students with disabilities and additional needs. Ensuring that any examinations taking place on sites are conducted in line with the awarding body's regulations.

questions.question: The College is preparing to become a Study Centre for an awarding body and is also planning a site redevelopment to accommodate more students. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what should happen?
options: Include the planned redevelopment in the resource plans; the Academic Board approves the decision
Leave the redevelopment out until it is complete; the Principal's Executive Group approves the decision
Include it in the resource plans; the awarding body's Link Tutor approves the College's new status
Leave it out of the resource plans; the Board of Directors approves the College's new status
questions.explanation: Site expansion or redevelopment still in the planning stages should be included in the resource plans, and the College's Academic Board approves the decision to make the College a Study Centre and confirms resources are adequate.
questions.source_excerpt: Future for site expansion or redevelopment or mode of delivery currently in the planning stages should be included to ensure that the planned growth in student numbers can be achieved and accommodated within the resource provision. Ensuring that the College's Academic Board approves the decision to make the College a Study Centre

questions.question: A lecturer teaches on a franchised and a validated programme. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, who monitors compliance with the written guidance on franchise procedures, and who monitors the validated programme's assessment structures?
options: Franchise: the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring; validated: the Registrar
Franchise: the Quality Department; validated: the Senior Quality Assurance Officer
Franchise: the awarding body's Link Tutor; validated: the External Examiner
Franchise: the Registrar; validated: the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring
questions.explanation: Compliance with the written guidance for franchised programmes is monitored by the Quality Department, while validated assessment structures are overviewed by the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring and monitored by the Senior Quality Assurance Officer.
questions.source_excerpt: Producing written guidance to College lecturers on all procedures to be followed in franchised programmes with compliance monitored by the Quality Department. ... the marking and moderation of summative assessments, which will be overviewed by the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring and monitored by the Senior Quality Assurance Officer.

questions.question: The Senior Quality Assurance Officer has confirmed with the awarding body's representative that a franchised programme's assessments have changed. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, which follow-up actions are required?
options: Retain records, log the changes in the Quality Department's register and put them on the website promptly
Retain records and upload the changes to the website once the next Examination Board approves them
Enter the changes in the institutional Risk Register and tell current students about them at the next induction
Forward the changes to the External Examiner, who must approve them before any records are kept
questions.explanation: Records of relevant communication must be retained, the changes entered in the Quality Department's register of collaborative programmes, and the changes uploaded to the College's website at the earliest available opportunity.
questions.source_excerpt: Records of relevant communication must be retained, and the changes entered in the Quality Department's register of collaborative programmes. Uploading any changes to the programme onto the College's website at the earliest available opportunity

questions.question: Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, how does the College's role in securing student feedback differ between franchised programmes and validated programmes?
options: Franchised: it leads on acquiring feedback alone; validated: the awarding body leads
Franchised: the awarding body collects all feedback; validated: responsibility is shared
Franchised: it shares the responsibility with the awarding body; validated: it leads
In both: student representatives lead, with the PEG only observing the feedback process
questions.explanation: For franchised programmes the College shares responsibility with the awarding body for securing student feedback, whereas for validated programmes it leads on acquiring feedback and responding to it.
questions.source_excerpt: Sharing responsibilities with the awarding body for securing student feedback about the franchised programmes that it offers. ... Leading on the acquisition of student feedback about the quality of its validated programmes and providing appropriate responses to points made and issues identified.

questions.question: For a validated programme the College designed, a colleague argues that its assessment regulations need meet only the College's own standards, as the College owns the programme. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is correct?
options: They need meet only College standards once the partner has validated the programme
They must conform to the External Examiner's own personal marking standards
They must still conform to the standards set by the awarding body
They need meet only the standards set in the Office for Students' framework
questions.explanation: The assessment guiding principles, which apply regardless of the type of provision, require all assessment regulations and procedures to conform to the standards set by the awarding body.
questions.source_excerpt: Assure that all regulations and procedures relating to assessment conform to the standards set by the awarding body. ... Regardless of the type of provision being offered, these principles shall always apply

questions.question: A proposal for a new validated programme was drafted by academic staff alone, with no student or employer input, and is heading to the internal approval event. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is the position?
options: It is acceptable, as the internal approval event replaces any wider consultation
It falls short, as staff, students and externals must be consulted in the process
It is acceptable, as the partner consults students and employers at validation
It is acceptable, provided the programme is aligned with QAA subject benchmarks
questions.explanation: For validated programmes the College must ensure staff, students and externals are consulted in the design process, in line with the principle that programme design includes input from staff, students and externals such as employers.
questions.source_excerpt: To ensure programme design includes input from staff, students, and externals such as employers and practitioners. ... The College will ensure that staff, students and externals are consulted in the process

questions.question: A draft annual monitoring report for a programme analyses grades and resources but omits staff feedback and the actions arising from a recent external review. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy's guiding principles, what should happen?
options: Nothing, as external review actions are reported separately to the awarding body
Staff feedback is optional, but the external review actions must be added
It is submitted as it is, with the omissions noted for next year's report
Staff feedback and the external review actions and good practice are added
questions.explanation: The annual monitoring principles require reports to include student and staff feedback, and actions and good practice arising from external reviews, so both omissions must be addressed.
questions.source_excerpt: All programmes must be monitored on an annual basis and include student and staff feedback, an analysis of grade and other academic performance indicators, learning, library and other resources available to staff and students. ... Actions and good practice arising from external reviews should be included in the monitoring reports

questions.question: A colleague says a programme the College hosts as a Study Centre need not feature in College monitoring, because the College does not teach it. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, what is correct?
options: It is considered by the CAMR, and the College monitors it through regular meetings
It is left to the awarding body's own annual report, as the College does not teach it
It is included in the CAMR only if anomalies have been reported to the awarding body
It is included in College monitoring once College staff begin teaching after year one
questions.explanation: All programmes, regardless of provision type, are considered by the CAMR, and for Study Centre provision the College monitors the programme through regular meetings, typically including awarding body staff.
questions.source_excerpt: Monitoring the programme through regular meetings, typically, including staff of the awarding organisation. ... All programmes, regardless of the provision type, are considered by the College Annual Monitoring Report (CAMR).

questions.question: The College is preparing a new validated programme with a partner. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, how are the programme's entry requirements set, and what must the College then do with them?
options: The College sets them alone after validation and publishes them once the first cohort enrols
The partner's standard requirements apply, and the College shares them with applicants on request
Agreed with the partner at the validation event, then clarified and publicised by the College
Agreed at the College's internal approval event, then held by admissions staff for internal use
questions.explanation: For validated provision the College and partner agree entry requirements during the validation event, and the College must clarify and publicise the entry requirements for each programme.
questions.source_excerpt: Clarify and publicise the entry requirements for each programme, including those requirements made by the awarding body ... The College and the partner will agree the entry requirements for admission during the validation event.

questions.question: For a validated programme that the College designed and manages, a manager proposes that the College appoint the programme's External Examiner itself. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, is this permitted?
options: Yes, as validated provision allows the College to adopt more ownership over the programme
Yes, provided the College's Academic Board approves the chosen examiner beforehand
No, as appointing the External Examiner is the awarding body's responsibility
No, as the Senior Quality Assurance Officer must make every such appointment
questions.explanation: Even though validated provision gives the College more ownership, the policy states that the appointment of the External Examiner is the responsibility of the awarding body.
questions.source_excerpt: Validated programmes provide the College with opportunities for designing, developing and managing their own programmes ... The appointment of the External Examiner is the responsibility of the awarding body.

questions.question: A partner asks the College to start delivering, fully online and as a franchise, a programme that is new to the College but already approved by the partner. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy, is College Academic Board approval needed?
options: No, as the awarding body has already approved its own programme for delivery
Yes, as all new programmes need it, whatever the mode of delivery
No, as online delivery falls outside the Academic Board's approval role
Only if College staff will set or first mark the programme's assessments
questions.explanation: The policy requires Academic Board approval for all new programmes, regardless of mode or method of delivery, so prior approval by the partner or online delivery does not remove the need.
questions.source_excerpt: Secure Academic Board approval for all new programmes, regardless of mode or method of delivery;

questions.question: Course information for a new franchised programme sets out the entry requirements but says nothing about Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) or complaints and appeals. Under the Collaborative Partnerships Policy's recruitment principles, what is the position?
options: It is complete, as RPL is a matter for the awarding body's own regulations alone
It is complete, as complaints information is given only once a student enrols
It falls short, but only RPL needs adding, as appeals are handled after enrolment
It falls short, as accurate information on RPL and complaints and appeals is needed
questions.explanation: The recruitment principles include providing accurate information on Recognition of Prior Learning and on the processes for complaints and appeals, so both are missing.
questions.source_excerpt: To publish clear and concise entry requirements and course information for admission and selection processes. ... To provide accurate information on the Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL); and processes for Complaints and Appeals.

questions.question: You are arranging the purchase of IT equipment and you hold shares in one of the suppliers bidding for the work. Under the Conflict of Interest Policy, whose approval is needed before you procure from them?
options: The Chair of the Assessment and Progression Board
The awarding body, requested through the Pearson portal
The finance team, after obtaining three competing quotes
The Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring
questions.explanation: The policy states that no employee or associate should procure goods or services where they have an interest in the other party without the approval of the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring.
questions.source_excerpt: No employee or associate of London Churchill College should procure goods or services where he or she also has an interest in the activity of the other party without the approval of the Head of Programme and Academic Monitoring.

questions.question: According to the Conflict of Interest Policy, which person is barred from acting as the sole or Senior/Lead invigilator for an examination?
options: Any member of staff who has not completed invigilation training that year
Any member of staff employed by the College for less than one academic year
Any person who has taught any of the candidates in the examination subject
Any person who is not a member of the candidates' own course team
questions.explanation: The policy states that no person who has taught any of the candidates in the examination subject may act as the sole or Senior/Lead invigilator.
questions.source_excerpt: No person who has taught any of the candidates in the examination subject may act as the sole or Senior/Lead invigilator.

questions.question: Your son has enrolled on an LCC qualification and is in the group whose assignments you normally assess. What does the Conflict of Interest Policy require?
options: You may assess his work as long as a colleague who is not related to him internally quality assures it
You must not assess him, and no family member may internally quality assure his work
You may assess his coursework but must not invigilate any examinations he sits
He must transfer to another course or group that you do not teach, assess or quality assure
questions.explanation: The policy states that a learner will not be assessed by a family member, and that internal quality assurance of that learner's assessments will not be undertaken by a family member either.
