questions.question: Which pairing of role and responsibility is correct under the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: Head of Student Engagement: reviews each external speaker and applies mitigating actions
Prevent lead: addresses the core questions for every event at least two weeks in advance
College oversight board: maintains records of speaker and event activity for the college
PEG: monitors these activities and reports outcomes to the college oversight board
questions.explanation: PEG monitors external speaker and event activities and reports outcomes to the college oversight board; the Prevent lead reviews risks, organisers address the core questions and the Head of Student Engagement maintains records.
questions.source_excerpt: PEG will monitor these activities and report outcomes to the college oversight board as appropriate.

questions.question: A lecturer's bona fide research on a controversial topic needs access to sensitive material through college systems. What does the External Speakers and Events Policy say will happen in such instances?
options: Senior management will put processes in place so the college keeps meeting the Prevent duty
The research must be paused until the college oversight board has approved each source used
The lecturer must carry out the research off-site and using personal devices only
Access will be refused, because college systems may not be used for controversial research
questions.explanation: The policy allows college systems to be used for bona fide teaching and research, and says senior management will put processes in place so the college maintains activity to meet the Prevent duty.
questions.source_excerpt: This would include using college systems and allowing access for bona fide teaching and research purposes. In these instances, processes will be put in place by senior management so that the college maintains activity to meet prevent duty.

questions.question: A proposed speaker does not incite violence but is known for campaigning to undermine other groups' fundamental democratic rights and freedoms. What does the External Speakers and Events Policy require of the college?
options: Allow the talk, since there is no broad right not to be offended by any speaker's views
Allow the talk, since only inciting hatred or violence is covered by the policy's principles
Ensure the speaker is not supported or promoted, as undermining such rights is covered
Allow the talk if it is restricted to staff and is not advertised to students or the public
questions.explanation: The college must ensure that individuals who seek to undermine a group's or an individual's fundamental democratic rights and freedoms are not supported or promoted, even where they do not incite violence.
questions.source_excerpt: The college has a responsibility to ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence against any individuals or groups, or seek to undermine a society's, a group's or an individual's fundamental democratic rights and freedoms, are not supported or promoted.

questions.question: While checking a proposed speaker, you learn that a students' union at another university refused them permission to speak. How does this relate to the core questions in the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: It is not relevant, as only refusals by institutions themselves, not student unions, count
It is relevant only if that refusal took place within the last twelve months before your event
It is not relevant, as refusals elsewhere are considered only in the post-event process
It is relevant, as the core questions cover refusals by a student body or union at another HEI
questions.explanation: A core question asks whether the speaker has been refused permission to speak publicly at other educational establishments or organisations, expressly including the student body or union at another HEI.
questions.source_excerpt: Has the speaker been refused permission to speak publicly at other educational establishments or organisations (including the student body / union at another HEI)?

questions.question: A colleague says the core questions in the External Speakers and Events Policy are only needed for large public events, not a small in-class guest talk. Which statement reflects the policy?
options: They must be addressed for each speaker and event activity involving the college
They apply only to public seminar programmes and corporate events, not in-class talks
They apply only when the expected audience is larger than fifty people
They apply only when the speaker has not previously spoken at the college
questions.explanation: The policy requires organisers to address the core questions for each speaker and event activity involving the college, including speakers engaged in routine unit or course delivery.
questions.source_excerpt: The core questions must be addressed by organisers of each speaker and event activity involving the college.

questions.question: A colleague asks what the procedures in the External Speakers and Events Policy ultimately aim to enable the college to do. Which answer reflects the policy's stated aim?
options: Ensure that no view likely to offend students or staff is ever expressed at college events
Limit external speakers to those employed by the college's awarding university partners
Monitor, manage and deal effectively with anyone being drawn into violent extremism
Ensure every external speaker is approved in person by the academic board before booking
questions.explanation: The policy states that the college's aim is to be able to monitor, manage and deal effectively with the Prevent strategy in respect of any individual being drawn into violent extremism and eventually terrorism.
questions.source_excerpt: The college's aim is to be able to monitor, manage and deal effectively with the prevent strategy in respect of any individual being drawn into violent extremism and eventually terrorism.

questions.question: For an external speaker event, the organiser concludes the core questions 10 days before the event and receives the Prevent lead's review outcome 8 days before. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, which requirement has been missed?
options: The review outcome deadline, as it must reach the organiser at least ten days before the event
The core questions deadline, as they must be concluded at least two weeks before the event
No requirement, as each step was completed more than one week before the proposed event
The review outcome deadline, as it must reach the organiser at least two weeks before the event
questions.explanation: Core questions must be concluded at least two weeks before the event, so 10 days is too late; the review outcome need only reach the organiser at least one week before, which 8 days satisfies.
questions.source_excerpt: These considerations must be concluded at least two weeks prior to the proposed event / speaker activity. ... The outcome of this review will be communicated to the event organiser at least one week prior to the proposed event date.

questions.question: A guest practitioner is engaged routinely for on-site unit delivery, but the organiser's core questions reveal that another college refused the speaker permission to speak publicly. What does the External Speakers and Events Policy indicate should follow?
options: Nothing further, as speakers in routine teaching never require senior-level consideration
The speaker is automatically barred, as a refusal elsewhere prohibits speaking at the college
Escalation to senior-level consideration, because a flag has been raised by the core questions
Referral to the student body, which approves speakers engaged in routine course delivery
questions.explanation: Routine teaching speakers are not generally expected to need the most senior approval, but engagement is escalated to senior-level consideration where the core questions raise flags, such as a refusal elsewhere.
questions.source_excerpt: The college considers that there would not be a general expectation that speakers involved with the college in routine teaching, learning, and research require the most senior level of approval at the college. ... Engagement is considered through a series of core questions and only escalated to senior level of consideration if flags are raised.

questions.question: An organiser completes the core questions for a speaker at a college seminar and none of them raises a concern. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, what happens regarding the Prevent lead's review?
options: The Prevent lead still considers a review, as this applies to any external speaker event
No review takes place unless the speaker declines to sign the external speaker statement form
The review passes to PEG, which carries it out in place of the Prevent lead for routine events
The organiser carries out the review personally and applies any mitigating action required
questions.explanation: The review procedure applies to any external speaker event: the Prevent lead considers a review to lessen possible risks, if any, whatever the outcome of the core questions.
questions.source_excerpt: For any external speaker event the prevent lead will consider a review to lessen possible risks (if any) posed by an external speaker.

questions.question: An external speaker's core questions raise no concerns, but the speaker declines to sign the external speaker statement form, saying it is unnecessary. What does the External Speakers and Events Policy require?
options: Nothing further, as the form is needed only where the core questions raise a flag
The speaker may instead email to confirm they have read the college's Prevent policy
The form may be replaced by a mitigating action from the Prevent lead's review
The speaker must still sign the form confirming they will abide by college policies
questions.explanation: Signing the statement form is a separate requirement for every external speaker, confirming they will abide by college policies and the freedom of speech statements; clear core questions do not remove it.
questions.source_excerpt: The external speaker must sign the external speaker statement form (appendix 1), confirming that they will abide by college policies and the statements on academic freedom and freedom of speech.

questions.question: An external speaker offers to sign a version of the statement form committing them only to the college's freedom of speech statements, with other college policies deleted. How does this compare with the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: It is acceptable, as the form exists only to confirm the freedom of speech statements
It falls short, as the form confirms they will abide by all relevant college policies
It is acceptable if the Prevent lead countersigns the amended version before the event
It is acceptable provided the organiser notes the amendment in the event records
questions.explanation: The statement form requires the speaker to confirm they will abide by all relevant college policies, including the statements on academic freedom and freedom of speech, not those statements alone.
questions.source_excerpt: The external speaker must sign the external speaker statement form (appendix 1), confirming that they will abide by college policies and the statements on academic freedom and freedom of speech. ... confirm that I will abide by all relevant college ... policies, including meeting statements on academic freedom and freedom

questions.question: College staff are organising a conference at a hired hotel venue with several external speakers. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, which statement is correct?
options: It is in scope, so core questions must be concluded at least two weeks before it
It is out of scope, as the policy covers only speakers appearing on college premises
It is within scope, but off-site events need the core questions only one week before
It is out of scope unless students are expected to attend the conference as audience
questions.explanation: The policy's proportionate approach covers events and speakers both off-site and on-site, so the organiser must conclude the core questions at least two weeks before the conference.
questions.source_excerpt: Taking a proportionate approach involves reviewing, assessing, and authorising events and speakers off and on-site. ... These considerations must be concluded at least two weeks prior to the proposed event / speaker activity.

questions.question: A course team invites an external speaker to lead a session on a controversial topic that some students may find offensive; nothing suggests incitement. What does the External Speakers and Events Policy expect of the organiser?
options: Cancel the session, as external speakers may not teach on controversial topics
Proceed with no assessment, as teaching on controversial topics is exempt from checks
Consider it in the core questions; learning on controversial topics is encouraged
Refer the topic to the college oversight board, which approves any controversial topic
questions.explanation: Whether the topic is controversial is one of the core questions the organiser must address, but the college encourages learning and assessment on potentially controversial topics, so controversy alone is not a bar.
questions.source_excerpt: The college encourages development and teaching by academic staff and curricula which extends the academy, challenging norms and conventional wisdom and viewpoints, involving learning and assessment on potentially controversial topics. ... Is the subject matter, topic, or title controversial if advertised to the public or within the college community?

questions.question: A student society is organising a speaker event, and a student representative says their welfare-policy training means the society need not address the core questions. Which is correct under the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: The representative is right, as trained representatives may approve society speakers
The Head of Student Engagement must address the core questions for student-led events
The Prevent lead must address the core questions, as student-led events are reviewed centrally
The society, as a recognised organiser, must address the core questions at least two weeks ahead
questions.explanation: The student body is a recognised organiser of events and speakers, and organisers must address the core questions at least two weeks before; representatives' training covers guidance on welfare policies, not an exemption.
questions.source_excerpt: The core questions must be addressed by organisers of each speaker and event activity involving the college. These considerations must be concluded at least two weeks prior to the proposed event / speaker activity. ... The college's student body is recognised as a potential organiser of events and speakers.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the Prevent lead's review from the post-event process under the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: The review sets sanctions on speakers; the post-event process applies mitigating actions
The review applies mitigating action to reduce risk; the post-event process informs sanctions
Both take place after the event, with the review assessing risk and the process setting bookings
The review is run by PEG; the post-event process is run by the Head of Student Engagement
questions.explanation: The Prevent lead's review identifies and applies a mitigating action to reduce risk, while the post-event process helps determine future planning, booking and any sanctions imposed after the event.
questions.source_excerpt: A mitigating action will be identified and applied to reduce the level of risk. ... A post-event process will be held to help formulate the responses and assist the college in determining how the future events are planned, the booking process, and or the type of sanctions which might be imposed post event.

questions.question: Two speakers are proposed: A holds lawful views many staff find objectionable; B urges audiences to use violence against a named group. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, which is correct?
options: B must not be supported or promoted; A's objectionable views are not generally unlawful
Both must be refused, as the college must prevent any speaker from causing offence
Both may speak, as freedom of speech protects every view expressed at academic events
A must be refused, but B may speak if the Prevent lead applies a mitigating action first
questions.explanation: Expressing views some find objectionable is not generally unlawful, but the college must ensure that those who incite violence against any individuals or groups are not supported or promoted.
questions.source_excerpt: It is not generally unlawful to express views or undertake research or teaching that some might find objectionable or offensive. ... The college has a responsibility to ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence against any individuals or groups ... are not supported or promoted.

questions.question: After an event, a concern about an external speaker leads to a referral to authorities beyond the college. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, how are the responsibilities divided?
options: The organiser meets the statutory duty; the Prevent lead keeps the event records
The Head of Student Engagement meets the statutory duty and informs the organiser
The Prevent lead meets the statutory duty; the organiser maintains the event records
PEG meets the statutory duty and reports it to the college oversight board
questions.explanation: The Prevent lead must meet the Prevent statutory duty where referrals are made beyond the college, while the organiser must maintain records of the speaker and event activity.
questions.source_excerpt: The organiser must maintain records regarding the speaker and event activity, recording the processes followed in decision-making and outcomes. ... The Prevent lead must meet the prevent statutory duty where referrals have been made to partners and or to authorities beyond the college.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a responsibility that the External Speakers and Events Policy places on the organiser of an external speaker event?
options: Concluding the core questions at least two weeks before the event
Maintaining records of the decision-making processes and outcomes
Communicating the review outcome a week or more before the event
Seeking the Prevent lead's advice if they have doubts or concerns
questions.explanation: The outcome of the Prevent lead's review is communicated to the organiser, not by them; concluding the core questions, keeping records and seeking the Prevent lead's advice are all organiser responsibilities.
questions.source_excerpt: The outcome of this review will be communicated to the event organiser at least one week prior to the proposed event date.

questions.question: A colleague proposes extra checks on every external speaker from one particular faith group, whatever the event. How does this fit with the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: It fits, provided the Prevent lead approves the extra checks in writing beforehand
It fits for public events only, as internal teaching sessions receive lighter checks
It fits wherever that faith group is named in the Prevent duty guidance as a concern
It does not fit; the procedures target no religion and follow a risk-based approach
questions.explanation: The policy's procedures are not directed at any specific religion or religious group, and the college takes a proportionate, risk-based approach rather than applying checks by faith.
questions.source_excerpt: The approach is based on taking a proportionate and risk-based approach, as advised in the prevent duty guidance. ... This policy and set of procedures are not directed at any specific religion, religious group or at the proponents of any other set of beliefs.

questions.question: A colleague describes the External Speakers and Events Policy as mainly a tool for keeping controversial speakers away. Which correction is supported by the policy's stated purpose?
options: It bars speakers from any group named in the Prevent duty guidance, whatever their topic
It restricts controversial speakers at public events but not in routine teaching
It aims to ensure that nobody at the college is offended by a speaker's views
It focuses expressly on ensuring the freedom of speech of external speakers and events
questions.explanation: The policy states that it accompanies the college's Prevent policy and focuses expressly on ensuring the freedom of speech of external speakers and events held in connection with the college.
questions.source_excerpt: It is intended to accompany the college's prevent policy and focuses expressly on ensuring the freedom of speech of external speakers and events held in connection with the college

questions.question: Rival groups plan to protest at a college debate with an external speaker, raising a risk of intimidation. Which sequence is consistent with the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: Address the risk in the core questions at least two weeks ahead; the Prevent lead's review applies a mitigating action
Address the risk in the core questions one week ahead; the Prevent lead's review then cancels the event automatically
Record the risk after the event in the post-event process; PEG then applies a mitigating action to future events
Record the risk on the statement form; the Head of Student Engagement then applies a mitigating action
questions.explanation: A likelihood of intimidation is a core question the organiser must conclude at least two weeks before the event, and the Prevent lead's review identifies and applies a mitigating action to reduce the risk.
questions.source_excerpt: These considerations must be concluded at least two weeks prior to the proposed event / speaker activity. ... Is there a likelihood of a situation arising in which people might experience harassment, intimidation ... A mitigating action will be identified and applied to reduce the level of risk.

questions.question: To save time, an organiser asks the external speaker to work through the core questions and to sign the external speaker statement form. Which part of this conflicts with the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: Asking the speaker to sign the form, which the organiser must sign on the speaker's behalf
Asking the speaker to address the core questions, which the organiser must address
Asking the speaker to sign the form, which may be signed only once the event is over
No part, provided both are concluded at least two weeks before the proposed event
questions.explanation: The core questions must be addressed by the organiser, who is responsible for making an informed assessment, whereas the statement form is signed by the external speaker.
questions.source_excerpt: Responsibility is placed clearly on the organiser of the event to make informed assessment ... The core questions must be addressed by organisers of each speaker and event activity involving the college. ... The external speaker must sign the external speaker statement form (appendix 1)

questions.question: An organiser plans to write up records for a speaker event only once the post-event process has ended. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, when should records of preparation and decision-making be kept?
options: Throughout, covering the processes followed in decision-making and the outcomes
Only after the event, as part of the post-event process run by the college
Only once the Prevent lead's review outcome has reached the event organiser
Only where the event has been escalated to senior level after flags are raised
questions.explanation: Records of preparation and decision-making are maintained throughout, and the organiser must record the processes followed in decision-making and the outcomes.
questions.source_excerpt: Records of preparation and decisionmaking will be maintained throughout. ... The organiser must maintain records regarding the speaker and event activity, recording the processes followed in decision-making and outcomes.

questions.question: HR organises a skills workshop for staff only, delivered by an external trainer. A colleague says the External Speakers and Events Policy covers student-facing events alone. Which statement is correct under the policy?
options: It is exempt, as the policy's duty of care is owed to students and not to members of staff
It is covered only if the trainer's subject would be controversial if advertised to the public
It is covered, as activities developing staff skills are listed, so HR must address the core questions
It is covered, but the Prevent lead rather than HR must address the core questions for staff events
questions.explanation: The policy lists extra-curricular or co-curricular activities that develop staff and students' knowledge and skills among college-connected events, and the core questions must be addressed by the organiser of each such activity.
questions.source_excerpt: Extra-curricular or co-curricular activities which supplement and develop staff and students' understanding of knowledge, skill, subject area, or discipline. ... The core questions must be addressed by organisers of each speaker and event activity involving the college.

questions.question: Students say a booked speaker's lawful views will offend them, and a separate group has threatened to intimidate attendees on the day. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, how should the organiser treat these two issues?
options: Cancel the event, as the likely offence to students is itself enough reason under the policy
Offence alone is no bar, but the likelihood of intimidation is a core question to address
Neither matters, as the speaker's views are lawful and freedom of speech protects the event
Leave both to the post-event process, which determines how any sanctions are to be imposed
questions.explanation: Freedom of speech gives no broad right not to be offended, so offence alone does not stop the event, but whether people might experience intimidation is one of the core questions the organiser must address beforehand.
questions.source_excerpt: Exercising academic freedom and freedom of speech does not establish a broad right not to be offended. ... Is there a likelihood of a situation arising in which people might experience harassment, intimidation, verbal abuse or violence, damage to person or property?

questions.question: The college runs a public seminar programme with a different external speaker each month. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, how should the organiser handle the core questions for this series?
options: Once for the whole programme, at least two weeks before the first seminar in the series
Once per academic year, when the seminar programme is approved by the Prevent lead
Only for speakers who have not already spoken at an earlier college seminar or event
For each speaker and seminar, concluded at least two weeks before each one takes place
questions.explanation: Public seminar programmes are college-connected events, and the core questions must be addressed for each speaker and event activity and concluded at least two weeks before each proposed event.
questions.source_excerpt: Public seminar programmes and corporate events. ... The core questions must be addressed by organisers of each speaker and event activity involving the college. These considerations must be concluded at least two weeks prior to the proposed event / speaker activity.

questions.question: After the core questions and the Prevent lead's review are complete, the speaker's organisation is added to the UK government's list of proscribed organisations before the event. Under the External Speakers and Events Policy, what now applies?
options: The speaker must not be involved in the event in any circumstances, despite the earlier review
The event may go ahead, as the review outcome had already been communicated to the organiser
The event may go ahead off-site, so that the college's own premises are not used by the speaker
The matter is left to the post-event process, which decides on any sanctions after the event
questions.explanation: Events and meetings must not, in any circumstances, involve speakers from organisations proscribed by the UK government, so a completed review or an off-site venue makes no difference.
questions.source_excerpt: Any activity relating to events and meetings must not, in any circumstances, involve speakers or support of speakers from proscribed organisations listed by the UK government.

questions.question: An external organisation books a college hall for its own conference; one of its speakers campaigns to undermine a group's fundamental democratic rights. The organisation says it is not a college event. Which is correct under the External Speakers and Events Policy?
options: The organisation is right, as externally booked and led conferences fall outside the policy
Nothing is required of the college, as views some find objectionable are not generally unlawful
The college's duty covers only speakers who incite hatred or violence, not this speaker
It is college-connected, and the college must ensure the speaker is not supported or promoted
questions.explanation: Externally booked and led conferences are listed among events connected with the college, and the college must ensure that those seeking to undermine a group's fundamental democratic rights and freedoms are not supported or promoted.
questions.source_excerpt: Externally booked and led conferences and events. ... The college has a responsibility to ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence against any individuals or groups, or seek to undermine a society's, a group's or an individual's fundamental democratic rights and freedoms, are not supported or promoted.

policies.title: Freedom of Speech Policy and Code of Practice

questions.question: A colleague tells you they are worried that a student may be being drawn into extremism. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, who should the concern be raised with?
options: The local Prevent Co-Ordinator directly, who will open a case without involving anyone at the College
The Head of IT, who will begin monitoring the student's College email and social media accounts
The Metropolitan Police, who must be informed before the matter is raised with anyone at the College
The Director of Studies, who will liaise with internal contacts and, if required, external agencies
questions.explanation: Concerns about a staff member or student in the context of extremism or terrorism should go to the Director of Studies, who liaises with internal contacts and, if required, external agencies such as the local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police.
questions.source_excerpt: If any staff or students are concerned about a staff member or student in the context of extremism or terrorism, they should contact the Director of Studies, who will liaise with relevant internal contacts and, if required, appropriate external agencies, potentially including the local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how does the College approach speech or writing that may be regarded as offensive or as challenging norms and conventional wisdom?
options: The College prohibits it, because its Duty of Care takes priority over free expression on campus
The College requires it to be approved in advance by the Director of Studies
The College will not, as far as reasonably practicable and within the law, seek to restrict it
The College permits it in research publications but does not allow it to be expressed in teaching
questions.explanation: The policy says the College will not, as far as reasonably practicable and within the law, restrict or deny free expression of viewpoints, and that this includes speech regarded as offensive or challenging norms.
questions.source_excerpt: the College will not, as far as is reasonably practicable and within the law, seek to restrict or deny the free expression of viewpoints. This principle incorporates those situations where speech or writing may be regarded as offensive or challenging of norms and conventional wisdom.

questions.question: A lecturer wants to research extremism-related materials while developing a new module. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what must they do?
options: Proceed without seeking approval, as academic freedom covers all research
Refer the proposed activity to the Prevent Steering Group for approval
Obtain written permission from the Metropolitan Police before starting
Notify their line manager, as no formal approval process applies
questions.explanation: The policy requires staff or students who seek to research sensitive or extremism-related materials to refer the proposed activity to the Prevent Steering Group for approval.
questions.source_excerpt: Staff or students who seek to research sensitive or extremism-related materials, must refer proposed activity to the `Prevent' Steering Group for approval.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, to whom does the College's Freedom of Speech Code of Practice apply?
options: All students, staff, Directors, external Committee members and visiting speakers, for all activities on any LCC campus
Students and academic staff, while scheduled teaching activities are taking place on an LCC campus
Visiting speakers and external Committee members, as staff and students are covered by separate codes of conduct
Staff and Directors, for work activities on any LCC campus, as students fall under the Student Handbook instead
questions.explanation: The Code of Practice applies to all students, staff, Directors, external Committee members and visiting speakers, and to all activities on any of the College's campuses.
questions.source_excerpt: The following Code of Practice applies to all students, staff, Directors, external Committee members and visiting speakers, and applies to all activities on any of the three current London Churchill College campuses.

questions.question: A student claims that using College IT to promote a non-violent extremist ideology is acceptable because no violence is involved. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, is the student correct?
options: Yes, the ban on using College IT covers violent extremism and not non-violent ideologies
Yes, provided the material is clearly labelled as the student's personal opinion
No, using College IT to promote either violent or non-violent extremism is forbidden
Partly, as promotion is permitted once the student's tutor has approved it in advance
questions.explanation: The policy forbids using the College's MIS, IT and social media for the instigation, promotion, planning or execution of violent or non-violent extremism, radicalisation or terrorism.
questions.source_excerpt: It is forbidden to use the College's MIS, IT and social media or other elements of the information management systems or processes for the instigation, promotion or planning or execution of violent or non-violent extremism, radicalisation, or terrorism in the name of ideology or belief.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, what statutory duty does the College recognise under the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015?
options: To have due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism
To refuse any external speaker whose views are considered controversial or offensive
To report any student who discusses political or religious topics directly to the police
To monitor staff and student communications for signs of dissent
questions.explanation: The policy states that under the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015 the College has a statutory duty to have due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism (the Prevent duty).
questions.source_excerpt: Under Section 26 of the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015, the College recognises its statutory duty to have `due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism.'

questions.question: You are reviewing plans for a student society event at LCC. According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, which feature would make the event likely to be unlawful?
options: A speaker presenting a view that most attendees are expected to find unpopular
A debate that challenges conventional wisdom on a controversial topic
A lecture containing material that some attendees may find objectionable
Content that creates an environment of fear, harassment or intimidation
questions.explanation: The policy says speech or events that create an environment of fear, harassment, intimidation or violence are likely to be unlawful, whereas views some find objectionable or offensive are not unlawful if within the law.
questions.source_excerpt: Speech or events that encourage people into terrorism, or create an environment of fear, harassment, intimidation, or violence ... are likely to be unlawful.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what does an external speaker confirm by signing the External Speaker Statement Form?
options: That they will cover the full cost of any security, stewarding or venue arrangements that their event requires
That they grant the College the right to record, edit and publish their presentation on its website and channels
That they will abide by College policies, the Academic Freedom and Freedom of Speech statements, and the Prevent duty
That they hold no criminal convictions in the United Kingdom or overseas and are not currently under investigation
questions.explanation: The form confirms that the external participant will abide by the College's policies, the statements on Academic Freedom and Freedom of Speech, and the requirements of the Prevent duty.
questions.source_excerpt: The external participant is required to sign the External Speaker Statement Form, confirming that they will abide by the College's policies and the statements on Academic Freedom and Freedom of Speech, and with the requirements of the `Prevent' duty.

questions.question: A staff member is found to have made defamatory comments online about LCC and one of its students. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what follows?
options: No action, as the comments are protected by the College's commitment to free speech
Disciplinary action, and the College draws attention to possible legal consequences
An informal reminder, as defamation is a matter for the courts rather than the College
A referral to the Prevent Steering Group, which decides whether the comments may stay
questions.explanation: Every stakeholder must not make libellous or defamatory comments about the College, its staff or students; disciplinary action will be taken and the College highlights possible legal consequences.
questions.source_excerpt: has a responsibility not to make libelous and/or defamatory comments about the College, its staff, or students. Disciplinary action will be taken against individuals ... who are found to have made libelous and/or defamatory comments. In addition, the College draws the attention of individuals to the possible legal consequences of their actions.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, what responsibility arises from LCC's Duty of Care to the health, safety and well-being of its students, staff and visitors?
options: Ensuring that speakers with controversial or unpopular views are not invited to speak at the College
Ensuring that speech and writing on campus is approved in advance by senior managers
Ensuring that staff avoid discussing political or religious topics in their teaching sessions
Ensuring that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence are not supported or promoted
questions.explanation: The policy states that, issuing from its Duty of Care, LCC must ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence, or undermine fundamental democratic rights and freedoms, are not supported or promoted.
questions.source_excerpt: Issuing from its Duty of Care to all members of the College community ... LCC has an attendant responsibility to ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence against any individuals or groups ... are not supported or promoted.

questions.question: A group of students stages a protest aimed at stopping an invited speaker from being heard at LCC. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how will the College respond?
options: It will apply its disciplinary processes, as appropriate, to such activity
It will take no action, as protest is itself a protected form of free expression
It will give informal advice, as disciplinary processes cover staff and not students
It will issue a warning, as discipline is reserved for unlawful speech
questions.explanation: The policy states that the College will apply disciplinary processes as appropriate in the event of protest or systematic activity aimed at preventing freedom of speech.
questions.source_excerpt: The College will apply disciplinary processes as appropriate in the event of actions of protest or systematic activity aimed at preventing freedom of speech.

questions.question: How does the Freedom of Speech Policy describe undertaking research on controversial topics?
options: As an activity to be avoided in order to protect the College's reputation
As an expected part of generating new knowledge and academic development
As an activity reserved for senior academic staff and not open to students
As requiring written approval from the Board of Directors in each case
questions.explanation: The policy affirms that research on controversial topics is an expected part of generating new knowledge and academic development.
questions.source_excerpt: The College affirms that undertaking research on controversial topics is an expected part of generating new knowledge and academic development.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, what responsibility does London Churchill College share with other Higher Education Institutions?
options: To protect and promote intellectual enquiry and freedom of expression within the law
To approve in advance all teaching materials that deal with controversial subjects
To ensure that no speech or writing on campus causes offence to any student or staff
To guarantee unrestricted freedom of expression, whether or not the speech is lawful
questions.explanation: The policy states that LCC, in common with other Higher Education Institutions, has a responsibility to protect and promote intellectual enquiry and freedom of expression within the law.
questions.source_excerpt: London Churchill College, in common with other Higher Education Institutions, has a responsibility to protect and promote intellectual enquiry and freedom of expression within the law.

questions.question: The Freedom of Speech Policy quotes the Education Act 1986. According to that provision, who must take reasonably practicable steps to secure freedom of speech within the law?
options: Individual lecturers, within their own teaching sessions only
Persons concerned in the government of the establishment
The local authority for the area where each campus is located
The students' union, on behalf of all members of the establishment
questions.explanation: The quoted Education Act 1986 provision places the duty on persons concerned in the government of any establishment to take reasonably practicable steps to secure freedom of speech within the law.
questions.source_excerpt: Persons concerned in the government of any establishment ... shall take such steps as are reasonably practicable to ensure that freedom of speech within the law is secured for members, students and employees of the establishment and for visiting speakers.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what is every LCC stakeholder, whether student, staff member, external speaker, Director or consultant, entitled to?
options: A guaranteed platform to present their views at any College event or meeting
Advance warning before any College activity that may challenge their beliefs
Freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and to hold opinions without obtrusion
Protection from hearing any views that they personally find offensive or unpopular
questions.explanation: The policy states that every stakeholder is entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and to hold opinions without obtrusion.
questions.source_excerpt: every stakeholder at the College - whether student, staff member, external speaker, Director, or consultant, etc. - shall be entitled to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, and to hold opinions without obtrusion.

questions.question: Which of the following laws does the Freedom of Speech Policy name as one under which some speech or writing may be deemed unlawful in England and Wales?
options: The Data Protection Act 2018
The Freedom of Information Act 2000
The Human Rights Act 1998
The Public Order Act 1986
questions.explanation: The policy names the Public Order Act 1986, alongside the Equality Act 2010 and the Prevent Agenda within the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015, as laws under which speech or writing may be unlawful.
questions.source_excerpt: Some speech or writing may be deemed unlawful under a range of laws in England and Wales. These include, but are not limited to, the Public Order Act 1986, the Equality Act 2010 and the `Prevent' Agenda within the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015.

questions.question: Which of the following does the Freedom of Speech Policy list as a characteristic protected under the Equality Act 2010?
options: Pregnancy and maternity
Criminal record
Socio-economic background
Immigration status
questions.explanation: Pregnancy and maternity is one of the protected characteristics the policy lists under the Equality Act 2010; the other options are not on that list.
questions.source_excerpt: The Equality Act 2010 incorporates protections of the following characteristics: age, disability, gender, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, and sexual orientation.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, what are the policies contained in the College's Prevent Strategy document designed to ensure?
options: That all student societies obtain police clearance before holding any meetings on campus
That neither internal stakeholders nor external speakers promote or support terrorist activities
That controversial subjects are removed from the curriculum before each academic year begins
That staff members' personal social media accounts are checked by the College every term
questions.explanation: The College has implemented policies in its Prevent Strategy document to ensure that neither internal stakeholders nor external speakers promote or support terrorist activities or extremist doctrine.
questions.source_excerpt: has implemented policies contained within the Prevent Strategy document to ensure that neither internal stakeholders nor external speakers promote or support terrorist activities or extremist doctrine.

questions.question: The Freedom of Speech Policy states that open and honest discussion can only occur if a range of views, including unpopular ones, are heard in what way?
options: Under formal debate rules
Only in closed seminars
With tolerance and respect
Through a neutral chair
questions.explanation: The College believes open and honest discussion can only occur if a range of views, including unpopular or offensive ones, are heard with tolerance and respect.
questions.source_excerpt: The College strongly believes open and honest discussion can only occur if a range of views, including those that are unpopular and offensive to some or many, are heard with tolerance and respect.

questions.question: Under the Code of Practice in the Freedom of Speech Policy, what responsibility do all staff and students have towards others?
options: To avoid voicing views others may find offensive
To report any disagreement to a line manager
To give notice before raising sensitive topics
To show consideration for others' dignity
questions.explanation: The Code of Practice states that all staff and students have a responsibility to show consideration for others' dignity.
questions.source_excerpt: All staff and students have a responsibility to show consideration for others' dignity.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what will each event involving an external individual or group to be staged at LCC be subject to?
options: A risk assessment, with clear questions to be answered by the organiser
A public consultation, with comments invited from all students
A police vetting check, with the results reviewed by the Board of Directors
A ballot of the student body, with a two-thirds majority needed to proceed
questions.explanation: Each event involving an external individual or group will be subject to a risk assessment, with clear questions answered by the organiser about the nature of the event.
questions.source_excerpt: each event involving an external individual or group to be staged at LCC will be subject to a risk assessment with clear questions to be answered by the organiser concerning the nature of the event.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, once a concern about extremism is raised, what else will occur, if deemed appropriate, alongside liaison with relevant contacts?
options: Immediate suspension of the person concerned
Signposting to welfare and support groups
A written warning placed on the person's file
Removal of the person's College IT access
questions.explanation: Alongside liaison with internal contacts and, if required, external agencies, the policy states that signposting to welfare and support groups will also occur if deemed appropriate.
questions.source_excerpt: Signposting to welfare and support groups will also occur, if deemed appropriate.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, which external agencies are named as potentially involved, if required, when a concern about extremism or terrorism is raised?
options: The Office for Students and the Charity Commission
The Information Commissioner's Office and Ofsted
The local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police
The Home Office and the local borough safeguarding team
questions.explanation: The Director of Studies liaises, if required, with appropriate external agencies, potentially including the local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police.
questions.source_excerpt: who will liaise with relevant internal contacts and, if required, appropriate external agencies, potentially including the local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police.

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, which College policy states expectations of use concerning the transmission or receipt of obscene, unlawful or indecent material?
options: The External Speaker and Events Policy
The Equality and Diversity Policy
The Student Code of Conduct
The Information Security Policy
questions.explanation: The policy states that the College's Information Security Policy sets out expectations of use concerning obscene, unlawful or indecent images or material, and mentions the Prevent duty.
questions.source_excerpt: The College's Information Security Policy clearly states expectations of use, concerning the transmission or receipt of obscene, unlawful, or indecent images or material

questions.question: According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, where is information on the consequences of accessing inappropriate material provided to students?
options: In the Student Handbook
In their offer letter
In the Prevent Strategy
On the College website
questions.explanation: The policy states that information about the consequences of accessing inappropriate material, and possible monitoring, is provided to students in the Student Handbook.
questions.source_excerpt: The Information Security Policy advises staff and students of the consequences of accessing inappropriate material ... This information is provided to students in the Student Handbook.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, staff and students are advised of steps the College may take regarding their communications. What may the College do?
options: Publish any communications that breach its policies
Monitor and/or intercept communications
Forward all communications to the Metropolitan Police
Delete all communications after an annual review
questions.explanation: Staff and students are advised, through the Information Security Policy, that the College may take steps to monitor and/or intercept communications.
questions.source_excerpt: The Information Security Policy advises staff and students of the consequences of accessing inappropriate material and the steps the College may take to monitor and/or intercept communications.

questions.question: Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, besides disciplinary action, what may follow, if necessary, from wilful contravention of the Code of Practice?
options: A public statement issued by the Board of Directors
Mandatory retraining overseen by the Prevent Steering Group
Recourse to law or external agency referral
Permanent withdrawal of all College IT and email access
questions.explanation: Wilful contravention leads to disciplinary action under the relevant student or staff procedure and, if necessary, recourse to law or external agency referral.
questions.source_excerpt: Willful contravention of this Code of Practice will lead to disciplinary actions being taken under either the Student Code of Conduct and Disciplinary Procedure or Staff Disciplinary Procedure, as appropriate, and, if necessary, by recourse to law or external agency referral.

questions.question: An outside campaign group whose aim is to undermine individuals' fundamental democratic rights and freedoms asks LCC to promote its activities. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how should the College respond?
options: It should not support or promote the group, a responsibility arising from its Duty of Care
It should promote the group, as free expression outweighs the College's Duty of Care in all cases
It should promote the group once its speakers have signed the External Speaker Statement Form
It should promote the group, provided its activities take place away from the LCC campuses
questions.explanation: Arising from its Duty of Care, LCC must ensure that individuals or groups who seek to undermine fundamental democratic rights and freedoms are not supported or promoted, whatever the setting or paperwork.
questions.source_excerpt: Issuing from its Duty of Care to all members of the College community ... LCC has an attendant responsibility to ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence against any individuals or groups, or seek to undermine society's, a groups or an individual's fundamental democratic rights and freedoms, are not supported or promoted.

questions.question: A manager believes the Education Act 1986 duty quoted in the Freedom of Speech Policy secures freedom of speech only for enrolled students. For whom does the quoted provision require freedom of speech within the law to be secured?
options: Students and employees of the establishment, but not any of its visiting speakers
Students only, as employees' speech at work is governed by their employment contracts
Members, students and employees of the establishment, and visiting speakers
Employees and visiting speakers, but not students while they are away from campus
questions.explanation: The quoted Section 43 provision requires reasonably practicable steps to secure freedom of speech within the law for members, students and employees of the establishment and for visiting speakers.
questions.source_excerpt: shall take such steps as are reasonably practicable to ensure that freedom of speech within the law is secured for members, students and employees of the establishment and for visiting speakers.

questions.question: A colleague says that, under the Freedom of Speech Policy, speech can only be unlawful if it breaches the Public Order Act 1986, the Equality Act 2010 or the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015. Is the colleague correct?
options: Yes, the policy presents those three Acts as the complete list of relevant laws
No, the policy says the relevant laws include, but are not limited to, those Acts
Yes, though the Education Act 1986 is also listed as a law that restricts speech
No, the policy says only the Equality Act 2010 can make speech or writing unlawful
questions.explanation: The policy says speech or writing may be unlawful under a range of laws which include, but are not limited to, the three named, so the list is not exhaustive.
questions.source_excerpt: Some speech or writing may be deemed unlawful under a range of laws in England and Wales. These include, but are not limited to, the Public Order Act 1986, the Equality Act 2010 and the `Prevent' Agenda within the Counterterrorism and Security Act 2015.

questions.question: A student society proposes to refuse membership to people because of their sexual orientation, claiming freedom of speech protects the decision. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how should this be regarded?
options: As protected, because freedom of speech at the College overrides the Equality Act 2010 duties
As permitted, provided the society publishes its membership rules to students in advance
As a matter for the Prevent Steering Group, which approves the rules of student societies
As discrimination prohibited under the Equality Act 2010 and contrary to College values
questions.explanation: Sexual orientation is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010, and the College affirms its duty regarding discriminatory activity prohibited under that Act, which is also contrary to its values.
questions.source_excerpt: The Equality Act 2010 incorporates protections of the following characteristics: ... and sexual orientation. The College affirms its duty to prescribe discriminatory activity or victimisation that is prohibited under this Act, which is moreover contrary to the College's values.

questions.question: A staff member tells a consultant working with LCC that they must not hold a particular religious belief while engaged on College business. What does the Freedom of Speech Policy say about the consultant's position?
options: Consultants are not College stakeholders, so the entitlement to hold beliefs does not reach them
Consultants are stakeholders entitled to freedom of religion and to hold opinions without obtrusion
The consultant's beliefs must first be declared to, and approved by, the Director of Studies
The entitlement applies to consultants only while they are working away from College premises
questions.explanation: The policy names consultants among the stakeholders entitled to freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and to hold opinions without obtrusion.
questions.source_excerpt: every stakeholder at the College - whether student, staff member, external speaker, Director, or consultant, etc. - shall be entitled to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion, and to hold opinions without obtrusion.

questions.question: A lecturer is organising a talk at LCC by a visiting author. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how are responsibilities for the risk assessment and the External Speaker Statement Form allocated?
options: The organiser answers the risk assessment questions; the author signs the Statement Form
The author answers the risk assessment questions; the organiser signs the Statement Form
The organiser completes both on the author's behalf, as visiting authors sign no College forms
The Director of Studies completes both, so neither the organiser nor the author is involved
questions.explanation: The organiser answers the risk assessment questions about the nature of the event, and the external participant signs the External Speaker Statement Form.
questions.source_excerpt: each event involving an external individual or group to be staged at LCC will be subject to a risk assessment with clear questions to be answered by the organiser concerning the nature of the event. The external participant is required to sign the External Speaker Statement Form

questions.question: A student's supervisor says only staff need approval to research extremism-related materials, so the student's dissertation research can start straight away. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, is the supervisor correct?
options: Yes, students need only their supervisor's agreement before researching such materials
Yes, as the Prevent Steering Group approval rule applies only to research proposed by staff
No, students must also refer the proposed activity to the Prevent Steering Group for approval
No, students must instead obtain written clearance from the Metropolitan Police beforehand
questions.explanation: The approval requirement applies to staff or students: anyone seeking to research sensitive or extremism-related materials must refer the proposed activity to the Prevent Steering Group.
questions.source_excerpt: Staff or students who seek to research sensitive or extremism-related materials, must refer proposed activity to the `Prevent' Steering Group for approval.

questions.question: During a talk at LCC, a visiting speaker makes defamatory comments about the College itself rather than about any individual. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how does the responsibility not to make defamatory comments apply?
options: It does not apply, as it covers comments about staff and students rather than the College
It does not apply, as visiting speakers are bound only by the External Speaker Statement Form
It applies only if the comments are repeated in writing or online after the talk has ended
It applies, as every stakeholder, including external speakers, must not defame the College
questions.explanation: Every stakeholder, expressly including external speakers, has a responsibility not to make libellous or defamatory comments about the College, its staff or students.
questions.source_excerpt: Each stakeholder at the College - whether student, staff member, external speaker, Director, or consultant, etc. - has a responsibility not to make libelous and/or defamatory comments about the College, its staff, or students.

questions.question: A student and a lecturer both wilfully contravene the Freedom of Speech Code of Practice at the same event. Under the policy, how will disciplinary action be taken?
options: Both under the Staff Disciplinary Procedure, as the Code of Practice is enforced by HR
Student Code of Conduct procedure for the student; Staff Disciplinary Procedure for the lecturer
Both under the Student Code of Conduct, as the contravention occurred at a student event
Prevent Steering Group review for the student; Staff Disciplinary Procedure for the lecturer
questions.explanation: Wilful contravention leads to disciplinary action under either the Student Code of Conduct and Disciplinary Procedure or the Staff Disciplinary Procedure, as appropriate to each person.
questions.source_excerpt: Willful contravention of this Code of Practice will lead to disciplinary actions being taken under either the Student Code of Conduct and Disciplinary Procedure or Staff Disciplinary Procedure, as appropriate

questions.question: A staff member believes the College's expectations about obscene, unlawful or indecent material on its systems cover only material they send, not material they receive. According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, is this right?
options: No, the Information Security Policy's expectations cover both transmission and receipt
Yes, the Information Security Policy's expectations cover only material that staff send
Yes, material staff receive is covered by the Student Handbook rather than by any policy
No, received material is covered, but only where it relates to the Prevent duty itself
questions.explanation: The Information Security Policy states expectations of use concerning the transmission or receipt of obscene, unlawful or indecent images or material, so receiving such material is covered too.
questions.source_excerpt: The College's Information Security Policy clearly states expectations of use, concerning the transmission or receipt of obscene, unlawful, or indecent images or material

questions.question: A concern about a student and extremism has been passed to the Director of Studies. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, when will external agencies such as the Metropolitan Police be involved?
options: In every case, as all extremism concerns must be notified to the police without delay
Never, as the policy requires such concerns to be managed entirely within the College
If required, with the Director of Studies liaising with them and with internal contacts
Only after the Prevent Steering Group has approved a referral to the external agency
questions.explanation: The Director of Studies liaises with relevant internal contacts and, if required, appropriate external agencies, potentially including the local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police.
questions.source_excerpt: they should contact the Director of Studies, who will liaise with relevant internal contacts and, if required, appropriate external agencies, potentially including the local Prevent Co-Ordinator and Metropolitan Police.

questions.question: An external group has spoken at LCC several times before, so the event organiser suggests skipping the risk assessment for its next event. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, is this acceptable?
options: Yes, a risk assessment is needed only the first time a group speaks at LCC
Yes, provided the group signs a new External Speaker Statement Form instead
No, but only because every external group needs fresh Prevent Steering Group approval
No, each event involving an external group must have a risk assessment
questions.explanation: The policy states that each event involving an external individual or group to be staged at LCC will be subject to a risk assessment, with no exception for repeat visitors.
questions.source_excerpt: each event involving an external individual or group to be staged at LCC will be subject to a risk assessment with clear questions to be answered by the organiser concerning the nature of the event.

questions.question: Students complain that a lecturer's lawful teaching on a contested historical topic includes views many of them find objectionable, and ask for it to be stopped. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what is the position?
options: Teaching that some find objectionable is not unlawful, providing it is within the law
Teaching that a majority of students finds objectionable is likely to be unlawful
Objectionable views may appear in research publications but not in taught sessions
The teaching must be paused until the Prevent Steering Group has reviewed its content
questions.explanation: The Code of Practice states that it is not unlawful to express views or undertake teaching that some might find objectionable or offensive, providing it is within the law.
questions.source_excerpt: It is not unlawful to express views or undertake research or teaching that some might find objectionable or offensive, providing it is within the law.

questions.question: A manager says LCC's Duty of Care, as described in the Freedom of Speech Policy, extends only to enrolled students. Whose health, safety and well-being does the policy say the Duty of Care covers?
options: Students and staff, but not visitors attending College events
All of the College's students, staff and visitors
Students only, as staff are protected by employment law
Staff and visitors, as students are covered by the Handbook
questions.explanation: The policy describes LCC's Duty of Care as ensuring the health, safety and well-being of all its students, staff and visitors.
questions.source_excerpt: Issuing from its Duty of Care to all members of the College community to ensure the health, safety, and well-being of all its students, staff and visitors

questions.question: LCC is asked to host two external speakers: one holds lawful views that many staff find offensive; the other is known to incite hatred against a religious group. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how should the College treat them?
options: Not seek to restrict the first speaker's lawful views, but ensure the second is not supported or promoted
Refuse both, as its Duty of Care requires it to shield staff and students from views they find offensive
Host both, provided each signs the External Speaker Statement Form and the organiser answers the risk questions
Refuse the first, but host the second if the risk assessment for that event identifies no safety concerns
questions.explanation: The College will not seek to restrict lawful viewpoints even where they are regarded as offensive, but its Duty of Care means individuals who incite hatred or violence against any group must not be supported or promoted.
questions.source_excerpt: LCC has an attendant responsibility to ensure that individuals or groups who incite hatred or violence against any individuals or groups ... are not supported or promoted. ... the College will not, as far as is reasonably practicable and within the law, seek to restrict or deny the free expression of viewpoints. This principle incorporates those situations where speech or writing may be regarded as offensive

questions.question: At a College committee meeting on an LCC campus, an external Committee member makes defamatory remarks about a named student. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, how does the Code of Practice apply?
options: It does not apply, as external Committee members are bound only by the committee's own terms of reference
It applies to external Committee members, and stakeholders must not make defamatory comments about students
It applies only to defamatory remarks about the College itself, and not to remarks about individual students
It does not apply, as the Code covers teaching and events on campus but not the business of committees
questions.explanation: The Code applies to external Committee members for all activities on any LCC campus, and each stakeholder has a responsibility not to make libellous or defamatory comments about the College, its staff or students.
questions.source_excerpt: The following Code of Practice applies to all students, staff, Directors, external Committee members and visiting speakers, and applies to all activities on any of the three current London Churchill College campuses. ... has a responsibility not to make libelous and/or defamatory comments about the College, its staff, or students.

questions.question: A visiting speaker refuses to sign the External Speaker Statement Form, arguing that the Education Act 1986 duty quoted in the Freedom of Speech Policy already protects visiting speakers' freedom of speech. What is the position?
options: The speaker is right, as the Act's protection for visiting speakers replaces the need for any College form
The speaker may go ahead unsigned, provided the organiser answers the risk assessment questions instead
The speaker may go ahead unsigned if the Director of Studies confirms the talk raises no Prevent issue
The Act secures speech within the law; the external participant must still sign the form
questions.explanation: The quoted Act secures freedom of speech within the law for visiting speakers, and the Code separately requires every external participant to sign the External Speaker Statement Form.
questions.source_excerpt: shall take such steps as are reasonably practicable to ensure that freedom of speech within the law is secured for members, students and employees of the establishment and for visiting speakers. ... The external participant is required to sign the External Speaker Statement Form

questions.question: A staff member says discrimination on the grounds of gender reassignment is not a concern under the Freedom of Speech Policy, because it is missing from the Code of Practice's list of grounds. What does the policy say?
options: The staff member is right, as only the grounds listed in the Code of Practice are protected at LCC
Gender reassignment is covered, but only under the Prevent duty rather than the Equality Act 2010
It is an Equality Act 2010 protected characteristic, and prohibited discrimination is against College values
Gender reassignment is protected only for staff, as students are covered by the Student Handbook
questions.explanation: The policy lists gender reassignment among the characteristics protected under the Equality Act 2010, and the College affirms its duty regarding discrimination prohibited by that Act, which is also contrary to its values.
questions.source_excerpt: The Equality Act 2010 incorporates protections of the following characteristics: age, disability, gender, gender reassignment, ... The College affirms its duty to prescribe discriminatory activity or victimisation that is prohibited under this Act, which is moreover contrary to the College's values.

questions.question: A lecturer repeatedly promotes extremist doctrine in class. Their manager says the College's Prevent policies target only external speakers and only terrorist activities. According to the Freedom of Speech Policy, is the manager right?
options: Yes, the Prevent policies apply to external speakers, while staff conduct falls under separate policies
No, they aim to stop internal stakeholders as well as external speakers promoting extremist doctrine
Yes, the Prevent policies address terrorist activities, while extremist doctrine is left to academic freedom
No, they cover internal stakeholders, but only students and not members of staff such as lecturers
questions.explanation: The Prevent Strategy policies aim to ensure that neither internal stakeholders nor external speakers promote or support terrorist activities or extremist doctrine, so a lecturer is covered.
questions.source_excerpt: has implemented policies contained within the Prevent Strategy document to ensure that neither internal stakeholders nor external speakers promote or support terrorist activities or extremist doctrine.

questions.question: During a seminar, a student makes remarks encouraging classmates to join a terrorist cause. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, which response by the lecturer is correct?
options: Treat it as offensive but lawful speech, as views that some find objectionable are protected
Refer the remarks to the Prevent Steering Group, which approves or rejects such content
Contact the Metropolitan Police directly, without informing anyone at the College
Treat the remarks as likely unlawful and raise the concern with the Director of Studies
questions.explanation: Speech that encourages people into terrorism is likely to be unlawful, and concerns about a student in the context of terrorism should be raised with the Director of Studies.
questions.source_excerpt: Speech or events that encourage people into terrorism ... are likely to be unlawful. ... If any staff or students are concerned about a staff member or student in the context of extremism or terrorism, they should contact the Director of Studies

questions.question: A student argues that, because the Freedom of Speech Policy says offensive views are not unlawful, their speech discriminating against others on the grounds of religion must also be protected. What is the correct position?
options: It is likely to be unlawful, as offensive views are protected only within the law
It is protected, as the policy treats religious views that offend others as lawful
It is protected, provided it is delivered in a debate heard with tolerance and respect
It is protected unless a formal complaint about it is made to the Director of Studies
questions.explanation: Offensive views are lawful only providing they are within the law, and speech that discriminates against others on the grounds of religion or belief is likely to be unlawful.
questions.source_excerpt: It is not unlawful to express views or undertake research or teaching that some might find objectionable or offensive, providing it is within the law. ... Speech or events that ... discriminate against others on the grounds of age, disability, gender, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, sexual orientation, race, religion, or belief are likely to be unlawful.

questions.question: To avoid causing offence, a staff member chairing a College debate plans to allow only views that most participants are likely to find acceptable. How does this plan sit with the Freedom of Speech Code of Practice?
options: It follows the Code, which asks staff to protect participants from unpopular or offensive views
It follows the Code, provided the chair records the excluded views and circulates them afterwards
It conflicts with the Code's view that open discussion needs unpopular views to be heard as well
It conflicts with the Code only if an external speaker is among those taking part in the debate
questions.explanation: The College believes open and honest discussion can only occur if a range of views, including those unpopular and offensive to some or many, are heard with tolerance and respect.
questions.source_excerpt: The College strongly believes open and honest discussion can only occur if a range of views, including those that are unpopular and offensive to some or many, are heard with tolerance and respect.

questions.question: An external speaker who signed the External Speaker Statement Form later tells the organiser that the Prevent duty applies only to College staff and students, not to guests. Under the Freedom of Speech Policy, what is the position?
options: The speaker is right, as the form covers College policies but not statutory duties such as Prevent
By signing the form, the speaker confirmed they would abide by the requirements of the Prevent duty
The speaker is right, provided the event has passed its risk assessment and no concern was raised
The Prevent duty binds guests only when their event has been referred to the Prevent Steering Group
questions.explanation: By signing the External Speaker Statement Form, the external participant confirms they will abide by College policies, the Academic Freedom and Freedom of Speech statements, and the requirements of the Prevent duty.
questions.source_excerpt: The external participant is required to sign the External Speaker Statement Form, confirming that they will abide by the College's policies and the statements on Academic Freedom and Freedom of Speech, and with the requirements of the `Prevent' duty.

questions.question: A staff member's wilful contravention of the Freedom of Speech Code of Practice is referred to an external agency. The staff member argues that internal discipline can no longer follow. Under the policy, is this right?
options: Yes, the policy treats external referral as an alternative to internal disciplinary action
Yes, once referred, the matter is handled under the Student Code of Conduct procedure instead
No, but the external agency must first give its consent before any internal action can begin
No, action under the Staff Disciplinary Procedure may be taken as well as any external referral
questions.explanation: Wilful contravention leads to disciplinary action under the relevant procedure and, if necessary, recourse to law or external agency referral; the two are not presented as alternatives.
